NVIDIA Dynamo

DSX OS AI Inference Workshop - Dynamo

Inference fundamentals, faster replicas with ModelExpress, cache-aware routing, KV cache movement, disaggregation and autoscaling, admission control, serving through failures, and Snapshot restore.

01

Inference fundamentals + scaling

Inference request processing, GPU memory allocation, prefix caching, single-worker deployment, performance metrics and scaling.

02

ModelExpress

A new replica takes too long to help: pull the weights from GPUs that already hold them, over NIXL, instead of reading storage again.

03

Dynamo Router

Why a second worker barely helped the slowest turns, then how the Dynamo router picks a worker: what workers report about their cache, how overlap and load become one cost, and the policy file that holds the knobs.

04

KVCR (KV Cache Runner)

A subagent lands on a worker that has never seen its context. KVCR copies that context from the worker that has it instead of recomputing it: how it works, a live demo, and early results on real workloads.

05

Disaggregation

Prefill and decode worker pools, KV-cache transfers, performance tradeoffs and deployment configuration.

06

Autoscaling

Planner scaling policies, latency targets and replica counts.

07

Admission control

Request rejection, queueing policies and session-aware admission under load.

08

Resiliency

Keep serving when something breaks: request migration and graceful shutdown keep requests alive, GPU Memory Service and Shadow Engine recover from software faults in seconds, and KVCR-Guard keeps the KV cache through an engine or GPU failure. Hardware faults come next, with Snapshot.

09

Snapshot

Checkpoint a warmed-up worker once, including GPU state, and restore it on any node in seconds. Together with ModelExpress: restore the engine, then wake with weights from a peer.

                  Coding-agent request flow

                  Agent

                  Holds the code, the user’s request and everything the session has produced so far. Decides what to send next and runs tools.

                  LLM server

                  Accepts requests over HTTP and returns model responses.

                  POST /v1/chat/completions
                  1code + user request
                  4the whole accumulated contextcode + request · prior responses · tool results · new instruction
                  2a response, which may ask for a tool call

                  3Run the tool

                  File contents, test output, an error message: more text for the context.

                  Repeat until the task is complete.One agent session is many inference requests, and each request carries the whole context so far.

                  Coding-agent request flow (1.5 min)

                  We'll use a coding agent as our workload throughout the workshop. The agent runs outside the model server. It keeps track of the task, sends requests to the model, and runs any tools the model asks it to use.

                  [click] For the first request, the agent sends the code and the user's instructions to the server through the chat completions endpoint.

                  [click] The model returns a response. In this example, that response asks the agent to run a tool.

                  [click] The agent runs it and collects the result. That could be the contents of a file, some test output, or an error message.

                  [click] For the next request, the agent sends the earlier conversation again, with that tool result and any new instructions appended.

                  [click] This repeats until the task is complete. So one agent session can generate many inference requests, and successive requests contain a lot of the same text.

                  That repeated context is important for serving. The server needs to process the new material, but we'd like it to reuse work it has already done on the shared prefix. We'll first look at where that work happens and what the server needs to keep in memory.

                  LLM serving architecture

                  LLM server

                  HTTP endpoint

                  Accepts prompts through the OpenAI-compatible API and streams generated tokens to the client.

                  POST /v1/chat/completions

                  vLLM engine

                  The serving stack tokenizes prompts. The engine uses continuous batching to schedule GPU forward passes and allocates KV-cache blocks.

                  GPUs

                  HBM stores model weights, KV cache and activations. GPU kernels execute attention and matrix multiplications. Performance depends on arithmetic throughput and memory bandwidth.

                  LLM serving architecture (1.5 min)

                  On the server side, the request first reaches an HTTP endpoint. That's the interface the agent talks to, and it's also where the generated tokens stream back to the client.

                  [click] Behind that endpoint is vLLM. Its serving stack converts the prompt into token IDs, and the engine schedules the work that will run on the GPUs.

                  It uses continuous batching, so requests can join or leave the batch as execution progresses. The scheduler decides which requests can run together, within the available compute and memory limits.

                  The engine also manages the KV cache. This holds the attention state computed for tokens in the context, so later computation can reuse it. vLLM allocates that state in blocks as requests need space.

                  [click] The GPUs hold the model weights and the working memory, and execute the model's kernels. Their arithmetic throughput determines how quickly they can perform calculations. Their memory bandwidth determines how quickly they can supply the data those calculations need.

                  To see how those limits affect a request, we need to separate prompt processing from token generation.

                  PrefillProcesses input tokens and builds the KV cache. Longer prompts require more work. Prefill and queueing contribute to time to first token.

                  DecodeGenerates one token per active sequence per step, reading model weights and updating the KV cache. Decode step time, scheduling and response delivery affect inter-token latency.

                  Prefill and decode (1 min)

                  When the server handles a request, it first processes the prompt and then generates the response. We call those two phases prefill and decode.

                  [click] During prefill, the model processes the input tokens and builds their KV cache. It can work on many prompt tokens together. A longer uncached prompt gives it more work to do before the answer can begin.

                  That delay contributes to time to first token. From the client's point of view, this also includes any time the request spends waiting in a queue.

                  [click] During decode, the model generates the response one token at a time. Each step uses the existing context and adds the new token's state to the cache, ready for the next step.

                  The time between those tokens determines how quickly the answer arrives once it has started. If several requests are running together, the engine schedules their generation steps together too.

                  So we need to watch both the wait for the first token and the speed of generation after that. A serving configuration can improve one without improving the other.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • This slide introduces ordinary autoregressive generation. Speculative decoding and chunked prefill do not need an aside here. Chunked prefill is addressed on the disaggregation contention slide.

                  GPU memory allocation (1.5 min)

                  GPU memory gives us a fixed budget, and the engine has to share it between the three uses shown here.

                  [click] First are the model weights. We load them when the worker starts, and every request uses that same copy. Adding another user doesn't require another copy of the weights.

                  [click] The engine also needs workspace to execute the model. That includes temporary activations and scratch buffers, along with memory for captured execution graphs when those are enabled. We have to allow room for this work before we decide how much cache the engine can support.

                  [click] The engine reserves part of the remaining memory for the KV-cache pool. This holds the attention state for the requests we're serving. As requests process more tokens, they need more blocks, so longer contexts use more of the pool.

                  [click] These users are all sharing that pool. We can fit more short requests, or fewer long ones, into the same amount of memory. If we keep adding requests, the engine eventually runs out of available blocks and has to make requests wait or reclaim space.

                  That's why memory is a serving budget. The weights determine part of the fixed cost, and the space left for KV cache helps determine how many requests we can keep active. More active requests can improve total throughput, but they also share the GPU's execution time, which can increase latency.

                  Memory tiers and bandwidth (1.5 min)

                  We can keep data in several places, but the GPU can't access all of them at the same speed. This chart compares the bandwidth available to read or move that data from each of them. The numbers are published hardware examples. Our workshop runs on H100s.

                  [click] On-chip SRAM provides very high bandwidth with limited capacity. GPUs use it for registers and caches. The Groq example here uses SRAM as its main working storage.

                  [click] HBM is the GPU memory we were just dividing up. It provides the capacity and bandwidth for model weights, execution buffers and active KV state.

                  [click] CPU memory gives us more space to retain cached context. Accessing that context requires data to cross the host-to-GPU connection, which takes time and consumes bandwidth.

                  [click] Flash storage adds more capacity again. It can hold checkpoints or retained context, but retrieving that data also depends on the storage system and the connection to it. The link rates shown here are limits, rather than measured storage read speeds.

                  [click] Another GPU may already have the data we need. A peer transfer can copy cached KV blocks or model weights directly between GPUs, using the available interconnect.

                  When we reuse cached state, its location matters. We save the work of recomputing it, but we may have to pay for a transfer. We'll use that tradeoff when we look at offloading and moving state between workers.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • The chart uses a logarithmic scale. Memory bandwidth is total bandwidth, while link bandwidth is shown per direction. The published platform specifications are not the workshop hardware configuration.

                  Prefix caching

                  Request 1code + user task
                  Request 2code + user taskassistant / tool-call responsetool result
                  shared prefixAlready processed for request 1. The server can keep that working state and reuse it.

                  Prefix caching (1.5 min)

                  Let's return to the two requests from our agent. The first contains the code and the user's task.

                  [click] The second contains that same text, followed by the model's response and the tool result. Only the end of the request has changed.

                  [click] The server has already computed the KV state for the shared prefix. If those blocks are still cached, it can reuse them for this request. It doesn't need to run the same prompt tokens through prefill again.

                  [click] It then processes the new context at the end. Those new tokens still attend to the cached prefix, so the model continues to use the full context. We've avoided recomputing the earlier state.

                  Reuse requires a matching token prefix. For an agent that makes many turns over the same code, this can avoid substantial repeated work. But the request needs to reach a worker that can actually access the cached prefix.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • The reuse depends on a matching token prefix. If an application changes text near the start of the prompt, the engine can lose reuse for the tokens that follow it. Keeping repeated instructions and tool definitions consistent helps preserve that match.

                  Cache locality and prefill latency (1.5 min)

                  Here's what happens when we route that second request to either of two workers. Both run the same model, but their caches contain different state.

                  [click] Server A handled the first request and still has its prefix cached. It can reuse those blocks, process the new context and begin generating the next response.

                  [click] Server B has no matching prefix. It has to process the full context before it can start generating. The client sent the same request, but this worker has more GPU work to do.

                  That can increase time to first token and consume capacity that could have served other requests. The actual latency also depends on how busy each worker is. A cached prefix is useful, but waiting behind a long queue can offset that benefit.

                  [click] So request placement needs to consider both cached state and current load. Round-robin routing doesn't account for the difference we're showing here.

                  Dynamo can route a request toward reusable state, and KVCR can make state available on another worker by transferring it. We'll cover both later. First, let's deploy a worker and see how Dynamo exposes it as a service.

                  Single-replica deployment (2 min, overlapped)

                  Let's deploy a single worker so we can see how the pieces we've discussed run on Kubernetes. This slide shows the checks we'll make, from applying the manifest to receiving a response.

                  We'll start with the DynamoGraphDeployment, or DGD. It specifies the frontend, the worker, and the model we want to serve. The complete manifest also pins the image and requests the GPUs the worker needs.

                  When we apply it, the Dynamo operator creates the resources needed to run those components. In the resource view, we can follow the Pods, Services and GPU allocation as the worker starts.

                  We'll wait for the deployment to become ready, then check that the model appears at the frontend's models endpoint. That tells us the worker has registered and the frontend can discover it.

                  Finally, we'll send a coding request and watch the response stream back. We'll leave this deployment running for the load tests.

                  This demo uses eager execution to reduce startup work. The performance measurements we'll discuss use a compiled profile. We'll apply the manifest now, then look at its configuration and startup time while the worker comes up.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • Run the keypress-controlled single-replica terminal demo. Follow its prompts to inspect the effective DGD, apply it, inspect resources, wait for readiness, query /v1/models and send a streaming request.

                  • Use the recording if startup overruns. The slide has no animation clicks.

                  • Pause the terminal demo after applying the deployment if the worker is still starting. Use slides 11 and 12 during startup, then complete readiness, model discovery and the streaming request once the worker is ready.

                  DynamoGraphDeployment configuration (2 min)

                  This is a shortened version of the deployment manifest. The DGD describes the serving components together, so we can configure and scale them through one Kubernetes object.

                  [click] The first component is the frontend. It exposes the OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint, routes requests to workers and streams responses back to the client. It runs separately from the worker and doesn't need a GPU.

                  [click] The worker runs the vLLM engine through Dynamo and registers itself so the frontend can find it. Here, we have one worker replica using two GPUs.

                  Tensor parallel size two means that those GPUs work together to run the model. It is still one serving replica. The language-model-only option makes this a text-only deployment for our coding workload.

                  [click] The operator watches this object and reconciles the resources needed to run it. On this cluster, that includes Grove resources, Pods, Services and GPU claims. Later, we'll increase the worker replica count in the DGD to add another instance of the engine.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  Worker startup latency (1.5 min)

                  Creating the worker Pod is only the beginning of startup. Before it can serve requests, the model has to be loaded and the engine has to be prepared.

                  [click] The bar separates three parts of that work. The first includes scheduling, image pulling and process startup. Loading the model means reading the checkpoint, preparing its tensors and copying them into GPU memory. The engine also has to allocate its cache and buffers, warm up kernels and, in this configuration, compile and capture CUDA graphs.

                  [click] In this recorded run, loading the weights took 267 seconds, and engine initialization took another 144. With the other startup work, the worker took eight minutes and thirteen seconds to become ready.

                  [click] These timings came from one run on two H100s, with the checkpoint on shared storage and compilation enabled. They'll vary with the deployment, but the breakdown shows why faster storage alone won't remove all of the delay.

                  That delay matters when we're adding capacity: the new worker can only take requests after startup finishes.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • The recorded run used Super VL with TP2, native loading from EFS and five-second readiness polling. Keep those details available for questions rather than reading the full measurement caveat aloud.

                  Inference performance metrics

                  Time to first tokenTTFT
                  How long before the answer starts arriving?
                  Generation speedinter-token latency · tokens/s per user
                  How quickly does the answer arrive once generation starts?
                  End-to-end request latencyrequest sent → last token
                  How long does the whole inference request take?
                  Throughputoutput tokens/s · requests/s
                  How much work does the service complete under this load?
                  Errors and unsuccessful requestserror rate · incomplete responses
                  Which requests fail to complete successfully?

                  Inference performance metrics (1.5 min)

                  Once the worker is ready, we need to measure how it behaves under load. The timeline follows a request from the moment we send it until the last token arrives.

                  [click] Time to first token measures how long we wait before the response starts. That includes time in a queue as well as prompt processing and transport overhead.

                  [click] After the first token, we measure how quickly the rest arrive. Inter-token latency is the time between tokens. Tokens per second per user expresses generation speed as a rate.

                  [click] End-to-end latency covers the whole request, including that initial wait and the time to generate the answer. Longer answers can take more time even when generation speed stays the same.

                  [click] Throughput measures how much work the whole service completes, usually in output tokens or requests per second.

                  [click] We also count requests that fail, time out or finish without a complete response. A throughput increase is less useful if more requests fail.

                  We'll use these measurements together, because a configuration can produce more tokens overall while making each user wait longer.

                  Per-user token rate versus throughput

                  Maximum throughput per megawatt

                  you gain Higher aggregate token throughput for the same power budget.

                  you give up Lower per-user token rate increases generation time for each agent turn.

                  pick it for Batch workloads: RL rollouts, evaluations and offline pipelines.

                  Maximum per-user token rate

                  you gain Higher per-user token rate reduces generation time for each agent turn.

                  you give up Lower aggregate token throughput per megawatt.

                  pick it for Interactive workloads with latency targets: coding assistants and customer-facing chat.

                  Per-user token rate versus throughput (2.5 min)

                  This chart shows why we need both throughput and per-user generation speed when we compare serving configurations.

                  [click] Each point is a measured configuration for the model and hardware shown here. Moving right means faster generation for each user. Moving up means more output tokens per second for the same power budget.

                  Take the point near the bend as an example: a P90 per-user rate of about 418 tokens per second at 8.3 million output tokens per second per megawatt. The leftmost point delivers about five times that throughput at half the per-user rate.

                  Batching helps explain the tradeoff. Processing more requests together can make better use of the GPU, increasing total throughput. But as the batch grows, each step can take longer, so each user's answer arrives more slowly.

                  [click] The configurations toward the left favor throughput. They can suit offline evaluations or rollouts where we care about completing a large amount of work. Those toward the right favor faster responses for interactive users.

                  The choice depends on the workload's latency requirements. We first decide how fast generation needs to be for each user, then choose the highest-throughput configuration that meets that requirement.

                  Agent concurrency and request queues (1.5 min)

                  We'll now increase the number of concurrent agents using the same deployment. To understand the resulting load, we need to follow the requests those agents produce.

                  [click] There are eight agent sessions in this example. Some are waiting for tools, while one has started three subagents. Together, they currently have seven requests in flight.

                  [click] Two of those requests are waiting in a queue. They haven't started executing, but that waiting time already contributes to their time to first token.

                  [click] The other five are in the engine's current batch. Some are processing prompts and others are generating output. They share the GPU's execution resources and KV-cache pool.

                  [click] So eight agents have produced seven outstanding requests, of which five are running. Those counts change as tools finish, subagents start and model responses complete.

                  That's why agent concurrency alone doesn't tell us how busy the engine is. We also need to inspect its active batch, queue and memory use.

                  Scaling: more traffic, same workload

                  More throughput, less speed per user

                  Throughput climbs

                  More requests share every forward pass, so the GPU produces more tokens per second in total, until it saturates.

                  Per-user speed drops

                  Each user gets a smaller slice of every step. Measure this over the time a user is actually generating.

                  Then TTFT climbs

                  Time to first token barely moves until requests start waiting for a slot, then it grows quickly.

                  Where it stops

                  Scheduler limits and KV capacity overlap. Run out of KV and the engine preempts requests and recomputes them. Don’t expect a smooth curve.

                  Shape only, not data. The real sweep at C16 to C128 on one and two workers is still running; C1 and C4 were single load points.

                  Explain the useful concurrency regime before showing its limits.

                  • GPU parallelism and engine batching let many requests share the GPU efficiently; as concurrency rises, aggregate throughput can increase while generation speed per user decreases. The service completes more work overall while becoming less interactive for each user.
                  • The regime has limits: scheduling and memory constraints can leave requests waiting, and insufficient KV-cache capacity can cause preemption and recomputation. Do not promise a smooth curve or that queuing begins only when KV cache fills.
                  • When the observed experience falls below the target, add serving capacity (next slides).
                  • Output tokens/s per GPU is resource efficiency; output tokens/s per user, over a clearly defined active generation window, is interactivity. Agents wait on tools, fork subagents and sit in queues, so never divide one by the session count to get the other.

                  The curve and load levels remain measurements to collect (load-sweep status report). Keep agent concurrency, active inference requests and queued requests distinguishable on any real plot.

                  KV-cache capacity and CPU offloading (1.5 min)

                  As we add agents, more requests need space for their context. This brings us back to the GPU memory allocation we looked at earlier.

                  [click] In this example, the weights and workspace stay the same size, while the requests fill the KV-cache pool.

                  [click] When the engine runs out of blocks, it can reclaim unused cached prefixes, keep new requests waiting or preempt running requests. If useful cached state is removed, a later request may need to recompute it. Both waiting and recomputation can increase latency.

                  [click] CPU offloading gives us somewhere else to retain reusable blocks. If a GPU copy is evicted, the engine can fetch an available copy from host memory instead of recomputing that prefix.

                  The transfer still takes time and uses the CPU-to-GPU link. Whether it helps depends on how that transfer cost compares with the prefill work it avoids.

                  The model still executes on the same GPU. Offloading lets us retain more cached state and can reduce repeated computation, but requests continue to share the same execution capacity. To add more execution capacity, we can add another worker.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • If asked about routing to offloaded blocks: the workers must publish the corresponding cache events for the router to account for CPU-resident KV.

                  Replica startup latency (1.5 min)

                  Let's increase the deployment from one worker to two.

                  [click] We change the worker replica count in the DGD and apply it. The operator starts another worker, which will register with the frontend once it's ready to serve.

                  [click] That new worker still has to load the model and initialize its engine. This is the same startup measurement we saw earlier, where the baseline worker took just over eight minutes to become ready.

                  [click] During startup, the original replica continues serving. Increasing the desired count doesn't immediately shorten its queue. That only becomes possible when the second worker can accept requests.

                  The existing replica already has the model weights in GPU memory. A compatible replica can provide those weights to the new worker, giving us an alternative to loading the checkpoint from shared storage again.

                  [click] Weight loading accounted for 267 of the 493 seconds in this run, so it is a substantial part of the delay. ModelExpress targets that part of startup. Later, we'll also look at Snapshot, which restores prepared engine state to reduce initialization work.

                  Prefill and decode resource contention

                  phase 1

                  Prefill

                  • Processes prompt tokens in parallel, possibly in chunks.
                  • Long prefills often saturate arithmetic throughput.
                  • Prefill contributes to TTFT, along with queueing and other overhead.
                  • Tune tensor parallelism and token batch size for the prompt workload.
                  phase 2

                  Decode

                  • One token per step for every active request, reading the weights and the KV cache each step.
                  • Small decode batches are often memory-bandwidth-bound.
                  • Generation step time contributes to inter-token latency.
                  • Tune parallelism and batch size for context length and concurrency.
                  Chunked prefill reduces decode stalls by interleaving smaller prefill chunks. Both phases still share GPU resources; disaggregation gives them separate scheduling and hardware budgets.Illustration shows unchunked prefill. Actual interference depends on the scheduler and workload.

                  Prefill and decode resource contention (2 min)

                  We've seen how to move cached state between workers. That also lets us run prefill and decode on different workers. To see why we'd do that, let's look at what happens when they share an engine.

                  [click] Prefill processes many prompt tokens together, so a large prefill can make heavy use of arithmetic throughput. Decode generates one token per active sequence at each step. At small batch sizes, reading the weights and KV cache often makes memory bandwidth the limiting factor. Those different demands give us a reason to tune the phases separately.

                  [click] In this timeline, A, B and C are already generating. Then request D arrives with a long prompt. The green block shows its prefill running as one uninterrupted step.

                  [click] While that step runs, A, B and C wait for their next tokens. Chunked prefill reduces this interruption by breaking the prompt into smaller pieces and interleaving decode. But the two phases still compete for the same GPU resources. Disaggregation gives each phase its own workers, so we can control their scheduling and capacity independently.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • The timeline deliberately illustrates unchunked prefill. Do not imply that current vLLM always runs a whole prompt in one blocking step.

                  Prefill and decode worker pools (1.5 min)

                  Here's what that separation looks like in a deployment.

                  [click] The client still sends its request to the frontend. The frontend coordinates the work across the two pools.

                  [click] The prefill workers process the prompt and produce the KV cache that decode will need. We can tune their parallelism and batching for the incoming prompt workload.

                  [click] The decode workers receive that cache over NIXL and generate the response. They have their own model weights and their own KV-cache capacity for active sequences. The tokens stream back through the frontend.

                  The diagram uses different tensor-parallel sizes to show that the pools can have different configurations. Those sizes are examples. The right settings depend on the model and workload.

                  [click] We can also change the number of workers in each pool independently. More incoming prompt work may require more prefill workers. Longer outputs or more concurrent generations may require more decode workers. We can even use different GPU types where the backend supports that configuration. The useful change is that we can allocate capacity to whichever phase needs it.

                  • The historical TP2-prefill / TP8-decode diagram is not the workshop layout. The workshop uses TP2 for both pools.

                  • Both pools retain model weights. Prefill may retain KV after handoff for prefix reuse.

                  Disaggregated request flow

                  AgentHTTP client

                  Sends a request.

                  Frontend① preprocess and route

                  Preprocesses the request, then picks a prefill worker and a decode worker for it.

                  Prefill worker② compute the KV cache

                  Processes uncached prompt tokens. Returns transfer metadata identifying KV blocks and the remote worker.

                  Decode worker④ receive KV, ⑤ decode

                  Fetches the KV blocks straight into its own GPU memory, then generates token by token and streams them back.

                  ③ Forward request and KV metadata
                  ④ KV blocks, GPU to GPUNIXL: configured GPU transfer backend. The cross-node demo uses LIBFABRIC over EFA.
                  ⑤ tokens stream back to the agent
                  Decode generation waits for the required KV. Transfer can overlap compute for other requests.

                  Disaggregated request flow (2 min)

                  Let's follow one request through the vLLM layout shown here.

                  [click] The agent sends its request to the frontend, which handles preprocessing and routing.

                  [click] The prefill worker processes the uncached part of the prompt. If it already has a matching prefix, it can reuse that state. It then returns metadata identifying the KV blocks and the worker that holds them.

                  [click] The frontend forwards that metadata with the request, so the decode worker can locate the state it needs. The KV-cache payload then moves between the workers.

                  [click] The decode worker allocates local cache blocks and uses NIXL to fetch the remote blocks into its GPU memory. In our cross-node demo, that transfer uses LIBFABRIC over EFA. The configured transport and available network devices matter here.

                  [click] Once the required cache is available, decode generates tokens and streams them back to the agent. A transfer can overlap compute for other requests, but this request's generation depends on its own cache being ready. That dependency is why the transfer path affects time to first token.

                  Disaggregation performance

                  scheduling isolation

                  Isolation

                  A long prompt runs on separate prefill GPUs, reducing interference with ongoing decode. Both pools still queue requests and use shared network resources.

                  per-phase configuration

                  Phase-specific parallelism

                  Prefill wants low tensor parallelism and token-heavy batches; decode wants high tensor parallelism and many concurrent sequences. One engine has to pick a compromise between them; two pools do not.

                  x prefill, y decode

                  Independent pool sizing

                  Prefill capacity follows uncached prompt work. Decode capacity follows active sequences, context lengths and output length. Profile both pools to choose their replica counts.

                  Disaggregation can improve throughput at a latency target. The gain is largest with long prompts, long outputs or high concurrency.

                  Disaggregation performance (1.5 min)

                  There are three ways this separation can improve performance.

                  [click] First, a long prefill runs on different GPUs from ongoing decode. That reduces the interference we saw in the timeline. Each pool can still queue work, and they can still compete for network bandwidth.

                  [click] Second, we can tune parallelism and batching separately. Prefill wants low tensor parallelism and token-heavy batches. Decode wants high tensor parallelism and many concurrent sequences. One engine has to pick a compromise between them; two pools do not.

                  [click] Third, we can size each pool for the work it actually receives. Prefill demand follows the uncached prompt tokens. Decode demand depends on how many sequences are active, how much context they have, and how long their outputs are. We need measurements of both to choose the replica counts.

                  [click] How much this helps depends on the workload. Long prompts, long outputs and high concurrency benefit most. The practical test is whether disaggregation meets our latency target more efficiently for the workload we intend to serve.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • The local Super VL result is a fixed-order, single-run observation. Repeated load sweeps are required for a capacity claim.

                  Disaggregated serving

                  What it costs, and when to skip it

                  the transfer

                  Every KV cache crosses the fabric once

                  Llama 3.1 70B, FP16 KV: 80 layers × 2 × 8 heads × 128 × 2 bytes is 320 KB per token, so an 8K prompt is about 2.6 GB.

                  NVLink, 450 GB/s each way≈ 6 ms
                  InfiniBand 400 Gb/s≈ 52 ms
                  100 GbE, TCP fallback≈ 210 ms

                  A few milliseconds vanish at hundreds of requests per second. A fifth of a second does not.

                  the plumbing

                  More to run and to size

                  • A second pool to size. Get the ratio wrong and prefill GPUs sit idle while decode queues, or the other way round.
                  • A router that pairs workers, discovery, transfer metadata, warm-up for cold transfers.
                  • On Kubernetes: RDMA device plugins, IPC_LOCK, and room in /dev/shm for NIXL.
                  the judgement

                  Leave it off when

                  • The model is small, prompts are short or concurrency is low.
                  • There is no fast fabric between the pools.
                  • One 8-GPU node serves a few hundred internal users: aggregated with prefix caching wins.

                  The docs say it plainly: in these cases an aggregated deployment is simpler and often faster.

                  Costs first, then the decision.

                  • Transfer: the whole KV cache of every request moves once. Size it for your model: per token, layers × 2 (K and V) × KV heads × head dimension × bytes. Llama 3.1 70B with GQA (8 KV heads) and FP16 is 320 KB per token, 2.6 GB for 8K tokens. Over NVLink that is a few milliseconds; over 400 Gb/s InfiniBand about 50 ms; over 100 GbE with the TCP fallback about 200 ms, which is why the operator guides call standard Ethernet too slow for this path.
                  • Plumbing: a router that pairs workers, discovery, backend-specific transfer metadata, warm-up (cold transfers inflate TTFT), RDMA plugins and shared memory on Kubernetes.
                  • When not to: small models, short prompts, low concurrency, no fast fabric. ClusterBid’s rule of thumb wants all of: models above 70B, 16 or more GPUs, InfiniBand or RoCE, sustained traffic. The Dynamo docs: an aggregated deployment is simpler and often faster in those cases.

                  Dynamo disaggregation configuration

                  spec: components: - name: Frontend type: frontend # routes, pairs prefill and decode - name: prefill type: worker subComponentType: prefill replicas: 1 args: [--model, nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4, --tensor-parallel-size, "2", --disaggregation-mode, prefill] - name: decode type: worker subComponentType: decode replicas: 1 args: [--model, nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4, --tensor-parallel-size, "2", --disaggregation-mode, decode]# both pools: same model, dtype, block size, KV layout# NIXL: sharedMemory 16Gi; RDMA resources across nodes

                  Encode, prefill and decode disaggregation

                  Encoder workers send embeddings over NIXL. In NVIDIA’s Qwen3.5 122B NVFP4 test, with 10 images and 1,024 output tokens, TTFT fell 50–58%, depending on encoder placement. Results depend on the workload.

                  Measured: same throughput, better tails

                  Super VL on four H100s, AgentX at concurrency 16: two aggregated TP2 workers against TP2 prefill + TP2 decode. Throughput unchanged (174.8 vs 174.4 tok/s); tails better (p99 TTFT 5.1 → 3.1 s, p99 ITL 20.3 → 10.7 ms); medians slower (p50 TTFT 255 → 317 ms). The demo shows one KV handoff; then back to aggregated serving.

                  Dynamo disaggregation configuration (1.5 min)

                  In the DGD, we keep the frontend and define separate worker services for prefill and decode.

                  [click] This service runs in prefill mode and has its own replica count.

                  [click] The other service runs in decode mode. In our demo, both use the same model revision and compatible cache settings, with two GPUs per worker. The workers also need the shared memory and transport devices required by their runtime. Our cross-node configuration uses EFA for NIXL transfers.

                  [click] We can apply the same idea to multimodal inference by separating image encoding from the language-model work. Encoder workers produce embeddings and pass them over NIXL. That can reduce interference for image-heavy traffic. The improvement shown here comes from a specific image workload and depends on how the encoder workers are placed.

                  [click] In the workshop demo, we'll check that prefill and decode run on distinct workers and that NIXL transfers complete. That verifies the serving path. Measuring its capacity requires repeated runs at increasing load, so we can see where each pool starts to queue.

                  Once we have separate pools, we also need a way to adjust their sizes as traffic changes. That's what the Planner does.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • Run the disaggregation demonstration after the fourth click. Verify separate worker identities and completed NIXL transfers in the logs and metrics.

                  • The demo uses TP2 in both pools, 64-token blocks, matching attention and recurrent-state layouts, and LIBFABRIC over EFA. Do not imply automatic TCP fallback.

                  • The encoder benchmark used Qwen3.5 122B NVFP4 with 10 images and 1,024 output tokens. Reported TTFT reductions were 58% with colocated encoders and 50% with a separate GPU tier; the separate tier added GPUs.

                  Dynamo Planner

                  Planner adjusts prefill and decode replica counts from traffic, engine metrics and configured targets.

                  Traffic and engine metrics

                  Traffic metrics plus per-iteration engine data: queued tokens, batch composition and execution time.

                  Target replica counts

                  Separate prefill and decode counts, using load thresholds or SLA targets and a performance model.

                  DGD replica updates

                  The Dynamo operator reconciles the updated replica counts. Planner itself runs as a service inside the same DGD.

                  Prefill and decode scale independently. Planner writes replica counts; the Dynamo operator reconciles the deployment.Configuration and defaults: Dynamo v1.5.1 Planner documentation.

                  Dynamo Planner (1.5 min)

                  As traffic changes, prefill and decode won't necessarily need to grow at the same rate. Dynamo's Planner automates those replica decisions.

                  [click] It reads traffic and engine metrics, including queued tokens, batch composition and execution time. These describe more than how many requests arrived. A request with a long prompt or a long output creates a different amount of work from a short one.

                  [click] The configured policy turns those signals into target replica counts. It can use load thresholds, or it can use a performance model to estimate the capacity needed for latency targets. Prefill and decode get separate counts, within the configured limits.

                  [click] The Kubernetes connector writes those counts into the DGD. The Dynamo operator reconciles the change and creates or removes the worker pods.

                  [click] So the Planner decides how much capacity to request, while the operator creates the resources. A new worker still has to start and become ready before it can serve traffic. That startup delay matters when we choose how early to scale. We're scaling manually in this workshop. The next slide explains the two scaling policies.

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

                  • No live Planner demonstration is scheduled. This slide explains the configured architecture; workshop replica changes are manual.

                  • Do not imply that Planner scale-down always drains in-flight requests. The behavior depends on the deployment path and version.

                  Snapshot

                  Cold start versus Snapshot restore, SGLang

                  Snapshot brings each replica up in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds, for weights from 1.5 GB to 913 GB, where a cold start takes a minute and a half to sixteen minutes.Restore clock: restore request to serving. Cold-start clock: process launch to engine initialization. Neither includes image pull or container start.

                  One representative figure from the Snapshot blog draft (read November 3) rather than its full benchmark matrix: SGLang, eight model and parallelism configurations on B200 with VAST storage. Restores took 3.6 to 42.7 seconds; the matching cold starts took 87 to 953 seconds.

                  ModelParallelismWeightsCold startSnapshot
                  Qwen3 0.6BTP11.5 GB87.1 s3.6 s
                  Qwen3 14BTP129.5 GB106 s5.6 s
                  Qwen3 14BTP229.5 GB125 s7.5 s
                  gpt-oss 120bTP165.3 GB269 s15.9 s
                  gpt-oss 120bTP465.3 GB240 s29.6 s
                  GLM-5.3 NVFP4TEP8464.8 GB427 s35.3 s
                  DeepSeek-V4.1 FlashTEP8510.3 GB953 s36.5 s
                  DeepSeek-V4-Pro NVFP4TEP8913.1 GB622 s42.7 s

                  Preserve the labels: the cold-start clock runs from process launch to engine initialization, the restore clock from the restore request to serving, and both exclude image pull and container-runtime setup. Do not call this fault-to-recovered-service time or a Super VL result. The draft’s inference benchmarks release the KV cache before checkpointing, so this is restoration of the initialized engine, not of an in-flight stream or the prefix cache.

                  The workshop’s own same-node Super VL TP2 control measured about 37 s agent restore and 40 to 41 s Pod-to-Ready from pre-staged NVMe (October 22), with a development build; requalify before using it as a live-demo claim.

                  The compile caches are files (compiler, kernel and autotune caches) copied into the new worker before its engine needs them. Graph capture and KV allocation still run, and no running process is restored: that is Snapshot, in resiliency.

                  Conditions: compiled benchmark profile, text-only Super VL 120B NVFP4 at TP2; every arm on the same two H100s with fresh private caches, fixed order, one run each, five-second Ready polling, host page cache not flushed. One idle source served both MX arms; its own storage start took 512 s, so the saving needs a compatible replica already running. The live demo is the eager profile (no compile step, so its engine init stays about 83 s); its three live runs reached Ready in 247 to 250 s, against 459 to 493 s from storage. The upstream deck’s “P2P alone saves 6%” was a B200 reading NFS at 22 GiB/s, where weights were already fast: the saving depends on how slow the storage path is.                   Cache-aware routing

                  Why didn’t more capacity help?

                  Coding agents with 12-turn sessions, about 80K-token prompts and a new turn every 45 s.

                  p90 turn latency · request to last token
                  One worker64 agents · 2 GPUs
                  33 s
                  One worker128 agents · 2 GPUs
                  140 s
                  Two, round-robin128 agents · 4 GPUs
                  113 s
                  Two, KV routing128 agents · 4 GPUs
                  54 s
                  past its limit

                  Twice the agents, one worker

                  p90: 33 → 140 s. Turns queue behind each other’s prefills, and the agents get 56% of the turns they ask for.

                  second worker

                  Round-robin: 113 s

                  Splits requests evenly, not work. One worker fell behind (61 running against 41), and 46% of turns missed some of their context.

                  cache-aware

                  KV routing: 54 s

                  Weighs cache overlap against load: workers even (55 and 55), 87% of turns where their context was, 35% more turns done.

                  Real AgentX traces, C32: round-robin let one worker queue up to 52 requests while the other held 7; KV routing kept queues at 3 or fewer.p95 time to first token: one worker 2.0 s · round-robin 11.5 s · KV 2.8 s. p90 turn latency: 44 s · 35 s · 29 s.

                  Outline 2.3 asks why more capacity did not improve the whole request experience. This is the measured answer, and it sets up the rest of the section: what the router knows about each worker’s cache, and how it weighs that against load.

                  • One worker at 64 agents: the slowest tenth of turns take 33 s (median 30 s). Double the agents on the same worker and they take 140 s (median 68 s); the worker serves only 56% of what the agents ask for.
                  • A second worker behind round-robin: the median turn drops to 45 s, but the slowest tenth still take 113 s. Round-robin splits requests evenly, not work: one worker averaged 61 running requests and the other 41, with twice the engine queue time, and 46% of turns ran on a worker missing some or all of their previous context (18% all of it).
                  • The same two workers behind KV routing: median 46 s, slowest tenth 54 s, and 35% more turns completed than round-robin. The workers stayed even (55 and 55 running) and 87% of turns ran where their context was.

                  TTFT p901.5 s49 s7.9 s4.4 s

                  Turns completed, minutes 3 to 9528575727978
                  Share of the requested turn rate103%56%71%96%

                  Both routers give the same median; the difference is the tail and the work done. Mean decode speed per user favors round-robin because it admitted fewer turns, so fewer shared each decode batch; it leaves out queueing and the first token, so do not present it as the routing comparison. Which round-robin worker falls behind is not predictable, so the tail gap will vary between runs.

                  Resiliency

                  Three questions for every failure

                  clientAgent

                  Streams a coding answer

                  no GPUFrontend

                  Routes each request and keeps its generated tokens for migration.

                  TP2 · 2 × H100Worker 1

                  TP2 · 2 × H100Worker 2

                  Ask of every failure

                  1Do the affected requests complete?or does the agent get an error

                  2When does usable capacity come back?serving traffic, not just Ready

                  3What happens to latency meanwhile?TTFT and per-user speed on the survivors

                  any fault

                  A request is cut off

                  Whatever fails, answers in flight stop part-way. Request migration finishes them on another worker; a planned restart drains first.

                  this section

                  Software faults

                  The engine process crashes or hangs; the GPU is fine. GMS keeps the weights in GPU memory and a parked Shadow Engine takes over in seconds.

                  next section

                  Hardware faults

                  A failed GPU takes its Pod down; Snapshot restores the engine from the node’s local disk (live demo). A lost node takes that disk too (slides only).

                  KVCR-GuardKeeps the KV cache in host memory, outside the engine: it outlives a crashed engine or a failed GPU, but not a lost node.

                  Opens the section with the outline’s three questions; ask them of every mechanism that follows, and keep completion, capacity and latency on the same timeline.

                  • Topology change, stated out loud: we leave disaggregation behind. Two aggregated TP2 workers behind one frontend, so a failure has one place to happen.
                  • A request is cut off whatever the fault, so request migration comes first. A planned restart drains instead.
                  • Software faults (this section): the engine process crashes or hangs while its GPU stays healthy. GMS keeps the weights and a parked Shadow Engine takes over. Shadow covers process faults only, not GPUs or nodes.
                  • Hardware faults (the next section): a failed GPU takes its Pod down, and Snapshot restores an initialized engine into the replacement Pod. The live demo deletes the worker Pod to stand in for the failed GPU. A lost node is slides only: cross-node restore is not qualified on our cluster.
                  • KVCR-Guard spans both: its pool is host shared memory owned by a sidecar, so by design it outlives a crashed engine or a failed GPU, but not the node. We tested the crashed-engine case. Its slides come right after Shadow, on the way to Snapshot.

                  About 1.5 minutes. Replaces the upstream “Every hop in the request path can fail” map, whose diagram is disaggregated and lists eight mechanisms the section does not cover.

                  Engine process recovery

                  The request survived. The capacity didn’t.

                  One engine killed with migration on, checked against the three questions.

                  question 1

                  Did the request finish?

                  Yes, within half a second. Migration moved it to Worker B and the answer completed.

                  question 2

                  When is the capacity back?

                  Minutes later. The restarted worker loads its weights and initializes again: 493 s for a new worker in section 1.

                  question 3

                  What happens to latency?

                  Everyone waits. In a published two-worker example, p50 TTFT rose to 23.8 s and 201 of 399 requests waited over 5 s for a first token.

                  Bridge from 3.1 to 3.2, per the outline: the request survives, but how quickly does the capacity return? Keep completion, capacity and latency on one timeline, using the opener’s three questions.

                  • Question 1, answered in the demo: migration resumed the stream on Worker B; the longest pause between chunks was 0.51 s.
                  • Question 2: the killed worker comes back only after a full startup. Section 1 measured 493 s to Ready for a new Super VL worker (267 s of weight loading, 144 s of initialization). A container restarted in the same Pod skips scheduling and the image pull, but still loads and initializes: about 7 minutes. Until then Worker B carries everything.
                  • Question 3: we have no matched latency measurement of our own. NVIDIA’s published two-worker example (GLM-5.2 NVFP4, B200, TP8): with a 283 s cold restart, p50 TTFT after the fault was 23.8 s and 201 of 399 requests waited over 5 s for a first token. The same numbers come back on the Shadow Engine slide, next to the fix.

                  Verbal cue for the next slide: capacity back in seconds needs the expensive parts (the weights, the initialization) ready before the failure.

                  The capacity chart is schematic: two workers, then one from the kill until the restarted worker is Ready, drawn at 493 s. It is not a measured capacity trace.

                  Why another model. Super VL TP2 has never reached a fault: the GMS reader rejects language_model.lm_head.input_scale (parameter shape (1,) against committed shape ()), and the writer hits a CUDA illegal memory access during FlashInfer warm-up (October 22; the same family of failures in the November 4–5 retry). Say it plainly: a preview feature with model-specific integration gaps is a useful thing to know before adopting it.

                  Evidence so far. November 9, this presenter (Qwen3-0.6B at TP1 on cp-0942): the standby served the first verified response 1.2 s after the kill, in the same Pod and GMS, with a new worker identity and a new standby confirmed. One request failed during the switch. Fallback recording: demos/transcripts/live/08-shadow-engine/20261109-a1. November 8 took 1.7 s with two failed requests (1.2 s in an earlier run that night); the October 22 control took 2.62 s.

                  Scope: process failures only, not GPU, Pod or node loss. The promoted engine starts with an empty KV cache, and in-flight requests need migration. Next: KVCR-Guard, for the cache.

                  Presenter implementation: the DGD Snapshot terminal demo (uv run python -m demos snapshot-dgd), after snapshot-dgd prepare and prime --auto --timeout 5400 offstage. The November 5 prime took 45 minutes: it creates the DGD, captures the initialized engine, stages and hash-checks a node-local copy, then restores the first worker and checks a coding request. Keep that DGD alive: its checkpoint belongs to its UID.

                  Framing: this is the hardware-fault case from the section opener. A failed GPU takes its worker Pod down; as long as the node survives, the replacement restores from the checkpoint on its local disk. On stage, deleting the Pod stands in for the failure. A lost node takes the local checkpoint with it, which is the shared-storage case: slides only.

                  If asked: the replacement here lands on the same GPU pair it was captured on; we have not run a restore onto a different GPU of the node.

                  On stage: show the checkpoint settings, delete the worker Pod (UID-guarded), watch the operator restore its replacement, check the identity table, then send a fresh coding request through the same frontend. The readiness wait sends no inference, so presenter pauses stay outside the clocks.

                  November 9 recording (cp-0124): agent restore 35.1 s (CRIU 19.4 s, CUDA 14.1 s), Pod-to-Ready 60 s, deletion-to-observed-Ready 63.3 s, then a correct coding response. November 5 measured 33.9 s, 59 s and 64.3 s. Separate boundaries, not a matched speedup against a cold start.

                  Fallback: demos/transcripts/live/04-snapshot-dgd/20261109-a1/main.txt. The pinned runtime still carries the destination identity/offline bridge overlay (reports/2026-11-04-snapshot-upstream-status.md). Any hardware, runtime or placement change needs requalification. The checkpoint released the KV cache before capture, so a restored worker starts with an empty cache.

                  Putting it together

                  What handles each failure, and what we showed

                  FailureWhat handles itStatusWhat we showed
                  Any fault, mid-answerRequest migrationopt-inliveSuper VL: streams finish on the peer, 4 of 4 under load
                  Engine crash or hangGMS + Shadow EnginepreviewliveQwen3-0.6B. Super VL is blocked on GMS bugs
                  Crash or failed GPUKVCR-Guardin developmenttestedSuper VL, engine killed: 4,224 tokens reused
                  A failed GPUSnapshot, local diskexperimentalliveSuper VL: Pod replaced, restored from local NVMe
                  A lost nodeSnapshot, shared storageexperimentalnot shownDiagram only: cross-node restore not qualified here
                  Any new replicaModelExpress + SnapshotexperimentalbenchmarkInternal: Qwen3-Next-80B on one B200, 180 s to 14 s
                  Several at onceThe full stack together—visionEach piece works alone; not tested together

                  The outline’s “return to the combined recovery story”: the section opener’s three kinds of failure, now with the evidence behind each. Migration continues requests; GMS and Shadow restore capacity after software faults; KVCR-Guard keeps cached context through an engine crash (and, by design, a failed GPU); Snapshot restores an initialized replacement Pod after a GPU failure the node survives; ModelExpress, from scaling, is the weight-loading path.

                  • Live: run on stage on our cluster. Tested: run on our cluster, not on stage. Benchmark: someone else’s measurement, labelled with its setup. Vision: a direction, not a tested composition.
                  • KVCR-Guard (November 4, nightly runtime): with one engine down, a request pinned to the peer pulled 6 blocks (99 MiB) from the Guard and reused 4,224 prompt tokens; the restarted engine then reused them locally. The first unpinned request failed with a 503, so automatic failover is not qualified. The live KVCR demo has Guard installed but injects no failure: it is not Guard evidence.
                  • Readiness, as the outline asks: Shadow Engine is a preview, the Snapshot project cautions against production-critical use, and KVCR-Guard is in development. Composition (for example, Snapshot shortening standby replenishment) is vision until it is tested.

                  speedup.json

                  Presenter implementation: the KVCR terminal demo (uv run python -m demos kvcr), after kvcr prepare and kvcr prime offstage. Prime takes about 15 minutes: 12 to start both engines, then a warm-up that sends each engine its first request (the one that pauses about 18 s after its first token) and opens the A-to-B transfer path. Start it early: each engine downloads the pinned nightly wheels when its container starts. A cut-off download failed two primes before the bootstrap began retrying it in place; leave time for a fresh run anyway. Each onstage step takes seconds of cluster time.

                  What to say. The router section ended with a choice: wait for the busy worker that has the context, or recompute it on an idle one. KVCR adds a third option: copy the context. Step 1: one DGD, engine A on cp-0198 and engine B on cp-0942; each Pod runs the engine (main) and a kvcr-services sidecar with its own EFA device, and the KV config adds a 4 GiB host pool and a kvcr tier over LIBFABRIC. Step 2: both workers are warm. Step 3: the main agent reads repository A on A, computed from scratch: about 2.4 s to the first token. Step 4: on B, repository B (the same size and question, but no worker has read it) takes about 2.5 s; repository A takes about 0.3 s, because B pulls 13 of its pages from A instead of recomputing them. Every answer names the file where the function was planted.

                  Close with the caveat, which the terminal no longer prints: this is tailored to show the mechanism (warm idle workers, one long shared prefix, requests pinned by hand). Under real agent traffic the gain depends on load and reuse; the next slide has results on real workloads.

                  Last live run, on the workshop placement (November 9, 09:19 UTC, cp-0198 to cp-0942), with the labels of the table on screen: A · repository A 2,435 ms, B · repository B 2,517 ms, B · repository A 317 ms: 7.94× on B. 54,912 tokens in 18 blocks, 0.29 GiB over EFA, matched on both ends; every answer named its planted file. Earlier runs: 8.38× on the same placement at 01:30 UTC (receipt reports/receipts/2026-11-09-kvcr-speedup-cp0942.json); with B on cp-0124, 7.84× (a3) and 8.37× (a2) on November 8, and seven extra rounds on warm workers 7.8–8.7×. Quote the numbers on screen. Fallback: the recording at demos/transcripts/live/07-kvcr/20261109-a1, in the current five-step flow.

                  Likely questions. Why so much faster? Recomputing 58K tokens is a full prefill; the copy moves 0.29 GiB and recomputes only the last partial page (Super VL is a hybrid Mamba-attention model, so its per-token KV cache is small). Always? No: with a short shared prefix the copy saves little (an earlier 6K-token version saved about 60 ms). Who chose B? We did, by pinning; router-to-KVCR hints are experimental in Dynamo 1.5. Guard? Installed in the Pods but not exercised here; it is in resiliency.

                  AIPerf

                  Benchmark any inference endpoint with production-shaped traffic, and get the metrics that decide your SLA.

                  pip install aiperfApache 2.0successor to GenAI-Perf
                  • AIPerf (github.com/ai-dynamo/aiperf) is a benchmarking tool that measures the performance of generative AI models served by any inference solution. It is a ground-up rewrite and successor to GenAI-Perf (NVIDIA developer blog, Sep 2026); docs/migrating.md calls it a drop-in replacement for currently supported features.
                  • Latest release v0.13.0 (Sep 24 2026): native Kubernetes execution (beta), speculative-decoding metrics, richer workload control.
                  Why it's hard

                  A benchmark that doesn't look like production tells you the wrong answer

                  Synthetic loadMooncake trace
                  success rate
                  100%
                  96%
                  tokens / s
                  22.5K
                  4.7K

                  Same server, two answers. Real prompt lengths and bursts cut throughput ~5× and exposed context-window failures that uniform synthetic prompts hide.

                  🧵
                  The client is the bottleneckad-hoc scripts are GIL-bound; AIPerf has to saturate a real server without slowing itself down
                  🎯
                  Throughput isn't goodputhigh tokens/s can hide that most requests missed their SLA
                  🧊
                  Cold starts liefirst requests warm caches and compile; they must not count
                  🤖
                  Agents aren't chatsmulti-turn sessions, subagents and tool pauses change KV reuse and load
                  • From docs/comprehensive-llm-benchmarking.md (written against AIPerf v0.5.0): the same deployment ran synthetic load at 100% success and 22.5K tokens/s, while replaying the Mooncake trace gave 96% success and 4.7K tokens/s and revealed context-window issues. "Trace-based testing exposes real-world challenges that synthetic benchmarks hide." "A system can have high throughput but low goodput if most requests miss SLAs."
                  • Client bottleneck framing from the NVIDIA developer blog "Benchmarking LLM Inference at Scale with AIPerf"; warm-up from docs/tutorials/warmup.md.
                  Architecture

                  Three planes, so measuring never gets in the way of sending

                  ~10 services in separate processes, talking over ZMQ. Press → to follow one request.

                  ① Credit. The Timing Manager sends a credit, permission to send exactly one request, to a worker.

                  ② Data. The worker reads its prompt from memory-mapped dataset files. No copies, no waiting.

                  ③ Request. The worker sends it to your server and timestamps every streamed chunk.

                  ④ Return. The credit goes back to the Timing Manager. A slow server means fewer free credits: natural backpressure.

                  ⑤ Records. Raw results go to Record Processors, which scale with load and compute per-request metrics.

                  ⑥ Results. The Records Manager aggregates and exports, alongside GPU and server metrics.

                  ZMQ pub/sub + ROUTER/DEALERwarm-up discardedsingle node or Kubernetes
                  • From docs/architecture.md. Control plane: SystemController, Timing Manager, Dataset Manager, Worker Manager ("decides what, when, and how many requests to send"). Data plane: Workers and the inference server. Analytic plane: Record Processors, Records Manager, GPU Telemetry Manager, Server Metrics Manager. A telemetry sidecar streams to OTel and MLflow.
                  • Why ZMQ: decoupling orchestration from execution keeps measurement accurate; workers spend their time on I/O and timing. Credits dispatch over ROUTER/DEALER with sticky sessions or least-loaded selection; returns come back on a PUSH/PULL fan-in.
                  • README says 10 services; the plugin registry now lists 12 including an optional API service, network-latency probe and a Kubernetes worker-group manager.
                  • Lifecycle: initialization → warm-up (discarded) → profiling → collection → processing → aggregation.
                  Load control

                  Shape the traffic exactly: closed loop, open loop, or replay a trace

                  Mode
                  Arrivals
                  --arrival-smoothness0.4

                  • From docs/cli-options.md. Concurrency (closed loop) issues a new request as soon as one completes; request rate (open loop) sends on a schedule and can be combined with --concurrency as a cap. Arrival patterns: constant, poisson (default), gamma, concurrency_burst; --arrival-smoothness (alias --vllm-burstiness) below 1 is burstier, above 1 smoother.
                  • Fixed schedule replays traces at their timestamps (automatic for trace datasets), with --replay-speedup. User-centric timing gives each simulated user a gap of num_users / qps between turns, designed for KV-cache benchmarking.
                  • The arrival strip is generated live from each distribution at 5 req/s; it shows shape, not a measurement.

                  AIPerf (1 min)
                  

                  We'll use AIPerf to generate the traffic and measure the responses in our load tests. It also runs the AgentX benchmark used by InferenceX.
                  

                  For an agent workload, replaying the request order matters. AgentX preserves dependencies between turns, pauses for tools and parallel subagent requests. That produces a different load from sending a stream of unrelated prompts.
                  

                  AIPerf records response timings and token counts so we can compare latency and throughput across runs. Throughout the workshop, we'll keep the coding-agent workload consistent and change the deployment. That lets us see what each serving change actually improves.

                  The deep dives · click one to jump
                  
  
                  Four questions every request answers
                  
  
                  

                  


                  

                  
  
                  Deep dive 1 of 4
                  
  
                  Performance
                  
  
                  Why is it fast, and how is it different?
                  

                  


                  

                  
  
                  The router · performance
                  
  
                  Send each turn back to the worker that holds its history
                  
  
                  Every chat turn resends the whole conversation. On the worker that already holds it, prefill only computes the new part. Follow two sessions, four turns each, taking turns.
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      1 square = 1 KV block (16 tokens) reused from cache computed in prefill
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
  
                  

                  


                  
  
                  
  
                  The router · performance
                  
  
                  Workers tell the router what they cache
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
                  ① Workers · GPU KV cache
                  
      
                  ② Event plane (ZMQ)
                  
      
                  ③ Router · radix tree of block hashes
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
  
                  

                  


                  
  
                  
  
                  Deep dive 1 · Performance 3/4
                  
  
                  Overlap meets load: lowest cost wins
                  
  
                  queued prefill+prompt−cache credit (overlap × weight)+decode load=costall in KV blocks · prompt = 64
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  balance · ITL
                  cache · TTFT
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  

                  


                  
  
                  
  
                  Deep dive 1 · Performance 4/4
                  
  
                  Disaggregation: two hops, or one when prefill can stay local
                  
  
                  Prefill goes where the cache is. Decode goes where load is low. With conditional disagg on (off by default), a request skips the prefill hop when the decode worker already holds most of the prompt, or when the prefill pool is busy.
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      conditional disagg
                  experimental
      request
                  
    
                  
    
    
                  
      
                  
      
                  
    
                  
  
                  

                  


                  

                  
  
                  Deep dive 2 of 4
                  
  
                  Fault tolerance
                  
  
                  What if a worker or the router fails?
                  

                  


                  
  
                  
  
                  Deep dive 2 · Fault tolerance 1/3
                  
  
                  Stop sending traffic to a dead or hung worker
                  
  
                  
    
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  1Local inhibition on
                  First failed request → the frontend skips that worker for 5 s. Instant, no coordination.
                  DYN_RUNTIME_INHIBITED_DURATION_SECS=5
                  
      
                  2Discovery on
                  Authoritative removal: EndpointSlice update, or the etcd lease expires. Its blocks leave the router's tree.
                  DYN_DISCOVERY_BACKEND=kubernetes | etcd
                  
      
                  3Canary health check opt-in
                  Idle 10 s → a tiny real inference, 3 s timeout. Catches an engine that hangs while its process looks alive.
                  DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_ENABLED=true
                  
    
                  
    
                  In-flight streams on the dead worker can migrate: the frontend resends prompt + generated tokens and the router picks a healthy worker (opt-in migration limit).
