                  Inside the Dynamo Router
                  
  
                  Admission control
                  
  
                  Why gate requests, and how: now, later, or never?
                  

                  


                  

  
  
                  Request admission and overload protection
                  
  
                  When offered load exceeds capacity, queueing increases latency. Admission policies can defer requests or return 529 to limit worker load.
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
      
                  
      
                  Illustrative: SLO = TTFT under 2 s; admission keeps workers at 80%.
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  
      
                  Admission policy mechanisms
                  ① Reject529
                  ② Queueclass queues
                  ③ ScheduleDRR
                  ④ Classifyrequest classifier
                  
    
                  
  
                  

                  Request admission and overload protection (1.5 min)
                  

                  When requests arrive faster than the workers can finish them, the queue grows and requests spend longer waiting. We may still be generating plenty of tokens, while more requests miss their latency target.
                  

                  The chart compares accepting all that work with limiting what reaches the workers. Goodput here counts requests that meet the time-to-first-token target. As offered load passes capacity, the illustration shows goodput falling without admission control. With admission control, excess work waits or gets rejected, keeping the admitted requests within the target.
                  

                  This is an illustration. The two-second target and eighty-percent admission limit are settings for this chart. A real deployment needs limits based on its measured performance.
                  

                  The four mechanisms below give us different controls. We can reject a request when all eligible workers are busy. Dynamo's default overload response is HTTP 529. We can hold requests in policy-class queues, then use deficit round robin to share service between those classes, accounting for their weights and uncached input tokens.
                  

                  Finally, a classifier can admit, defer or reject a request before it enters the router queue. We'll use that last mechanism to make decisions across an agent's whole session.
                  

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):
                  

                  • Move the offered-load slider from below 100% to above 100% while discussing the chart. This is an interactive control, not a deck-progress CLICK cue.
                  

                  • Worker-busy thresholds must be configured. Queue limits and ordering are configurable; deficit round robin arbitrates between classes, while ordering within each class is a separate policy.
                  

                  • HTTP 529 does not implement client retries. Clients need an appropriate backoff or alternate-endpoint policy.
                  

                  • The classifier runs before the router queue. In a disaggregated topology, remote prefill may have begun earlier, so avoid claiming it always runs before any inference work.

                  Deep dive 4 · Customization 3/4
                  
  
                  A scorer in 12 lines, shipped in 4 steps
                  
  
                  
    
                  struct LeastBusy;
impl WorkerScorer for LeastBusy {
  fn required_worker_inputs(&self) -> WorkerInputs {
    WorkerInputs::LOAD }          // or CACHE, PREFERRED_TAINT
  fn score(&mut self, _c: &WorkerSelectionContext<'_>,
           cands: WorkerCandidates<'_>, costs: &mut [f64])
           -> Result<(), WorkerSelectionPolicyError> {
    for (w, c) in cands.iter().zip(costs) {
      *c = w.load().ok_or_else(||
             WorkerSelectionPolicyError::failed("no load"))?
           .active_requests() as f64; }
    Ok(()) } }

                  Recap
                  
  
                  The story in four lines
                  
  
                  
    
                  1 · Performance
                  An exact cache view from KV events, scored with load in one cost, decided inside the frontend. Disaggregation routes prefill by cache and decode by load.
                  
    
                  2 · Fault tolerance
                  Requests migrate off dead workers. Every router replica is active and rebuilds its view from events after a restart. Sessions rebind when their worker disappears.
                  
    
                  3 · Admission control
                  Keep overload out of the engines: reject fast with 529, hold in policy classes, share by DRR, and decide with a RequestClassifier.
                  
    
                  4 · Customization
                  One policy YAML. Plug in Rust filters, scorers, and pickers, or run the router and its parts outside the frontend.

                  Request-level routing and session memory
                  
  
                  Dynamo’s KV router places requests using cached-prefix overlap and worker load. Request-level placement does not reserve capacity for an agent session’s future turns.
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
                  KV cache between agent turns
                  
      
                  agent 12 · tool34 · tool56 · tool78 · toolno room
                  
      
                  working set ≈ N × contextk
                  
      
                  Between turns, prefix blocks may remain in HBM for reuse or eviction. The estimate above assumes similar context lengths and excludes shared-prefix reuse.
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  KV cache eviction
                  When reusable context exceeds cache capacity, useful blocks can be evicted. Later turns must recompute the missing prefix; full eviction requires a full prefill.
                  
      
                  No tool-boundary backpressure
                  Request-level admission can hold or reject requests. Session-aware admission also tracks whether a session is between turns or still generating, so it can defer the next turn without interrupting decode.
                  
    
                  
  
                  

                  Request-level routing and session memory (1.5 min)
                  

                  Remember the agent loop from the start of the workshop: the model answers, the agent runs a tool, and then it sends another request with the accumulated context. The inference request ends at each turn, but that context can still be useful on the next one.
                  

                  That's what the rows on the left show. Some agents are generating and others are running tools. Their cached prefixes can remain in GPU memory between turns. With similarly sized contexts, the total working set grows roughly with the number of sessions times the context per session, before accounting for shared prefixes.
                  

                  Dynamo's KV router considers both cached-prefix overlap and worker load when placing each request. That helps reuse the cache, but it doesn't reserve enough space for every session's future turns.
                  

                  If useful context exceeds cache capacity, blocks get evicted. When those sessions return, the missing prefixes need prefill again. Under enough load, we're spending more compute rebuilding context that we already processed.
                  

                  Session-aware admission gives us another option: let the current model turn finish, then hold the session's next request. We can limit the sessions competing for cache without interrupting a generation already in progress.
                  

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):
                  

                  • Cached prefixes are evictable, not permanently reserved. A cache miss may be partial; full eviction requires a full prefill.
                  

                  • The rough N × context estimate excludes shared-prefix reuse. Available host or remote cache tiers can also change the amount of recomputation.
                  

                  • All content enters automatically; this slide has no deck-progress click steps.

                  Session-aware admission
                  
  
                  Dynamo’s experimental ThunderAgent plugin adapts the paper’s scheduler inside the frontend. It tracks sessions and token counts to estimate their logical context sizes.
                  
  
                  
    
                  active
                  paused
                  
    
                  reasoninga model turn is pending or running
                  
    
                  GeneratingThe engine is working on this program’s turn.
                  
    
                  Marked to pauseFinishes the turn, then stops at the tool boundary.
                  
    
                  actingbetween model turns
                  
    
                  Acting, cache reusableIts cached blocks remain subject to the engine’s eviction policy.
                  
    
                  PausedThe next model request waits. External tool work can continue.
                  
  
                  
  
                  
    
                  Tool boundary → actingThe scheduler can defer the next inference request while the agent runs a tool.
                  
    
                  Memory pressure → pauseHold the next request; let in-flight decode finish. If pausing ACTING programs is insufficient, mark running programs to pause after their current turn.
                  
    
                  Capacity available → resumeSelect programs that fit, favoring smaller contexts within each admission group, then pack them onto workers.
                  
  
                  

                  Session-aware admission (1.5 min)
                  

                  Dynamo's experimental ThunderAgent plugin adds that session-level decision inside the frontend. It groups requests by session ID and uses their token counts to estimate how much context each session carries.
                  

                  The table separates two questions. The rows describe what the session is doing. In the reasoning row, a model turn is pending or running. In the acting row, the model turn has finished and control is back with the agent, often while a tool runs.
                  

                  The columns describe whether the scheduler is allowing that session to continue. An active session's next request can proceed. A paused session's next request waits, while any external tool work can continue.
                  

                  Under memory pressure, the scheduler first pauses sessions that are already between model turns. If that isn't enough, it can mark running sessions to pause when their current turn finishes. It doesn't stop decode halfway through an answer.
                  

                  Pausing changes what the scheduler admits. The engine still decides when cached blocks are reused or evicted. When the estimated demand falls, the scheduler can resume sessions that fit on the available workers. The next slide shows how it makes that capacity decision.
                  

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):
                  

                  • The native plugin runs inside the frontend and is experimental. This script describes that implementation, not the older standalone Python router.
                  

                  • ACTING means the model turn has completed; it is not direct instrumentation of every external tool's lifecycle.
                  

                  • Session token counts are logical accounting, not measurements of physical KV blocks. Admission state is local to the plugin instance.
                  

                  • Selection favors smaller contexts within each admission group; do not describe it as an unconditional globally smallest-first policy.

                  Session utilization and admission thresholds
                  
  
                  Uworker = Σ (active-program tokens + buffer)  ÷  GPU KV capacity in tokensU estimates active-session demand, including token buffers.
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  0.80 · pause target
                  
    
                  0.85 · projected resume limit
                  
    
                  0.95 · pause threshold
                  
    
                  U = 0.70
                  
    
                  1.00
                  
  
                  
  
                  
    
                  U > 0.95: pause
                  Pause smaller ACTING programs first, aiming for 0.80. Running turns can be marked to pause after completion.
                  
    
                  Paused-session accounting
                  Paused programs leave the active estimate. Their cached bytes may remain until the engine reuses the space.
                  
    
                  Projected U < 0.85: resume
                  Normal resume includes the candidate’s token count and buffer. The 0.10 gap reduces repeated pause/resume cycles.
                  
  
                  
  
                  Resume: select and pack programs across workers, accounting for token buffers and worker pinning. A 30-minute default timeout releases a waiting request if a worker is live; downstream queues and deadlines still apply.
                  

                  Session utilization and admission thresholds (1.5 min)
                  

                  For each worker, the scheduler adds up the token counts of its active sessions, including a buffer for each one, and divides that by the GPU's KV-cache capacity in tokens. Active includes sessions that are generating and sessions between turns.
                  

                  That gives us the utilization estimate at the top. It's an estimate of the context we're allowing to stay active. It can differ from physical memory use because sessions may share prefixes or have cache stored elsewhere.
                  

                  The three markers show the default thresholds. Above ninety-five percent, the scheduler starts pausing smaller sessions that are between turns, aiming to bring the estimate down to eighty percent. If necessary, it also marks running sessions to pause after their current turn.
                  

                  A paused session leaves that active estimate. Its cached bytes can still be present until the engine reuses the space, so the number can fall before physical memory use changes.
                  

                  To resume a session normally, its context and buffer must fit while keeping projected utilization below eighty-five percent. That leaves a gap below the pause threshold, reducing the chance that we immediately pause it again. The scheduler uses those estimates to select sessions and place them on workers with enough headroom.
                  

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):
                  

                  • Native defaults: pause when U > 0.95; pause toward 0.80; normal resume requires projected U < 0.85, using a 0.10 gap below the pause threshold.
                  

                  • The utilization estimate includes ACTIVE reasoning and acting programs plus per-program token buffers. The implementation can weight acting programs. Its denominator is GPU KV capacity, not GPU plus host offload capacity.
                  

                  • Worker pinning constrains placement. Resume selects candidates within admission groups and packs the selected programs across workers.
                  

                  • The footer describes a separate default 30-minute deferral timeout. It releases a waiting request when a worker is live; downstream queues, eligibility and client deadlines still apply. It does not guarantee an end-to-end completion deadline.
                  

                  • There are no native Python-prototype soft-demotion or one-second priority-boost controls in this implementation.

                  Session scheduling benchmark results (1.5 min)
                  

                  These are two reported evaluations, each with its own model, hardware and baseline. On the left, the SWE-bench workload gained twelve to sixteen percent throughput over KV-aware routing alone.
                  

                  The table on the right shows why concurrency matters. At thirty-two to a hundred and twenty-eight concurrent RL rollouts, throughput was similar to the baseline. At a hundred and ninety-two to two hundred and fifty-six, model-token throughput was eleven to fourteen-point-six percent higher. At the highest concurrency levels, the baseline's throughput dropped sharply while the session-aware scheduler's throughput continued to rise.
                  

                  The reported prefix-cache hit rate stayed above ninety-four-point-five percent across that RL sweep. That is the behavior this policy is trying to preserve: enough useful context remains available that later turns can reuse it, leaving more compute for new work.
                  

                  For a deployment, we would measure throughput and latency across increasing session concurrency, alongside cache reuse and repeated prefill. That tells us whether session admission helps with our workload and how much waiting it introduces.
                  

                  We've now covered how to add capacity, divide it between prefill and decode, and control the work we admit. Next, we'll look at what happens when workers fail.

      NVIDIA Dynamo · KVCR
      
                  Distributed KV Cache Management with Dynamo Router and KVCR
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
    
                  
  
                  
  
                    
    
                  • Distributed KV cache management with the Dynamo Router and KVCR (KV Cache Runner).
                    • 
    
                  • The idea in one line: the router plans where KV should be, and KVCR moves it between workers.
                    • 
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  The problem
                  Three requirements for KV cache management
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
                  1
                  Avoid recompute
                  
        
        
                  Store KV in cheaper tiers and bring it back instead of recomputing.
                  
      
                  2
                  Avoid hot spots
                  
        
        
                  One popular prefix shouldn't pin all its traffic to one worker.
                  
      
                  3
                  Recover failures
                  
        
        
                  Losing a worker shouldn't mean recomputing its whole cache.
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                    
    
                  • Store and retrieve, avoid hot spots, assume failures.
                    • 
    
                  • 1. Avoid recompute: offload KV down the tiers (HBM → DRAM → remote storage) and retrieve it instead of recomputing.
                    • 
    
                  • 2. Avoid hot spots: many requests with the same prefix pile onto the one worker that holds it while others sit idle.
                    • 
    
                  • 3. Recover failures: when a worker dies its cache is lost and another worker has to recompute it.
                    • 
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Dynamo’s approach
                  Router plans. KVCR acts.
                  
    
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
    
                  
  
                  
  
                    
    
                  • Others: the router is load and KV aware, but a separate KV cache manager decides on its own where KV goes.
                    • 
    
                  • Dynamo + KVCR: 1) the router is hint-aware — it takes signals from the client; 2) it plans KV moves and sends them as hints that ride on requests; 3) the KVCR library inside each worker carries them out, moving KV between workers.
                    • 
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Planning
                  Plan early, with the full picture
                  
    
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
    
                  
    
                  The router sees one request at a time, so t2 queues behind t1 on busy Worker A while B sits idle.With signals, the router plans ahead: KVCR copies t1’s KV to B early, so t2–t4 run there.
                  
  
                  
  
                    
    
                  • Engine keeps the hot tiers. Router plans early. KVCR moves the KV.
                    • 
    
                  • Today the router uses cache and load to route this request, then the next. t2 lands on Worker A behind t1, which is busy, while Worker B is idle.
                    • 
    
                  • Next, the router as scheduler: it also takes signals from the workload and builds a forward plan. It has KVCR copy t1’s KV to Worker B ahead of time, so later turns (t3, t4) run on B.
                    •

                  KVCR in action
                  Sharing G2 across workers
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
    
                  
    
                  
      The router finds the KV. KVCR brings it to the worker that needs it. Press → to step through.
      1 · The router knows where the KV is: t2’s blocks sit in Worker B’s G2.
      2 · The plan rides on the request as a hint: fetch t2 from B.
      3 · A’s KVCR pulls the blocks from B’s G2, peer to peer.
      4 · A’s engine loads them into G1 and runs t2 without recomputing.
    
                  
  
                  
  
                    
    
                  • The router finds the KV. KVCR brings it to the worker that needs it.
                    • 
    
                  • 1) The router knows where the KV is. 2) The hint rides on a request. 3) Worker A’s KVCR pulls from Worker B’s G2, peer to peer. 4) A’s engine loads it into G1.
                    • 
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  KVCR-Guard · try it in development
                  Recovering from failures
                  
    
                  
  
                  
    
                  
      
    
                  
    
                  
      The DRAM pool sits in its own container, KVCR-Guard, so it can outlive the engine.
      The engine fails and G1 is lost. The pool survives. The guard confirms the engine is dead — a timeout alone isn’t enough to take over.
      The backup serves the pool. Worker A copies the KV from B’s pool, peer to peer, instead of recomputing it.
      The engine comes back and refills G1 from the pool — a copy, not a recompute — then a fenced handoff returns control.
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  On our cluster (Super VL, requests pinned): with one engine down, its peer pulled 6 blocks (99 MiB) from the Guard and reused 4,224 prompt tokens. After handback, the restarted engine reused them locally.
                  
  
                    
    
                  • The pool sits in its own container (KVCR-Guard), so it can outlive the engine. A backup KVCR waits on standby.
                    • 
    
                  • Engine fails: B’s G1 is lost but the G2 pool survives. The guard confirms the engine is dead before taking over; a timeout alone is not enough.
                    • 
    
                  • Backup serves the pool: the router sends t2 to Worker A with a hint to fetch from B’s pool; the backup KVCR serves it peer to peer.
                    • 
    
                  • Engine returns: it refills G1 from the pool (a copy, not a recompute), and there is a fenced handoff back to the engine.
                    • 
    
                  • On our cluster (November 4; Super VL TP2 on one node; Dynamo 1.7.0.dev20261103 wheels on the workshop base): A’s EngineCore was killed and held down. A request pinned to B pulled 6 blocks / 103,809,024 bytes from A’s Guard and recorded 4,224 external-cache input tokens, with no failed deliveries. After handback, the replacement A reused 4,224 of 6,050 input tokens from its own pool, with no remote deliveries.
                    • 
    
                  • Boundary: the first unpinned request after the fault failed with HTTP 503 (the frontend picked the dead endpoint three seconds before discovery removed it; migration was off). Not qualified: automatic failover, in-flight migration, cross-node recovery, GMS composition. The live KVCR demo has Guard installed but injects no failure, so it is not Guard evidence. Source: reports/workshop-kvcr-guard-qualification.md.
                    •

                  Primitives
                  Programmatic KV Cache Control
                  
  
                  • Section: the primitives the router can use to control where KV lives — copy, invalidate, no retain, move, prefetch, and topology-aware placement — driven by hints from the agent harness.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  KVCR · the subagent case
                  Copy: fork KV for a sub-agent
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  The harness spawns a sub-agent that forks session S1. Press → to step.1 · The harness sends a hint: S1 forks into a sub-agent, 48k in, ~350 s of work.2 · A is busy, so the router load-balances to B and picks copy.3 · KVCR copies S1 from A’s G2 into B’s G2. B has free KV space and the copy is likely to be reused.
                  S1 in HBMS1 in DRAMtemporaryfreedother sessions
                  
  
                  
  
                  Back to the question the router section left open. The main agent’s context sits on A, A is busy, and B has room. The router can wait for A or recompute the whole context on B. KVCR adds a third option: copy the context to B.
                  • Step 1: the harness announces a subagent fork. Harness hints are roadmap.
                  • Step 2: the router sends the request to B with a copy hint. Router-to-KVCR hints are experimental in Dynamo 1.5.
                  • Step 3: KVCR copies S1 from A’s host pool (G2) into B’s, and B loads it into HBM for the request instead of recomputing it.
                  The demo, next, has this shape: the main agent reads repository A (58K tokens) on A, and B pulls its pages from A over EFA instead of recomputing them. There we pin the requests by hand.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Primitives · Invalidate
                  Invalidate: drop context that isn’t needed
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  The harness compacts S1’s context. Press → to step.1 · The harness reports compaction: 96k becomes 8k, keeping the summary and the tail.2 · The old blocks are dead on both workers. The router frees every dead copy.
                  S1 in HBMS1 in DRAMtemporaryfreedother sessions
                  
  
                  
  
                  • Invalidate: drop context that isn’t needed.
                  • Harness metadata: session S1, event compaction, ISL 96k → 8k, keeps summary + tail, next turn in ~80 s.
                  • The router knows the old blocks are dead and that copies exist on A and B, so it picks invalidate.
                  • A frees the old context in G1 and G2 and keeps the summary; B frees its stale copy in G2.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Primitives · No retain
                  No retain: use it once, leave nothing behind
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  A one-off turn on S1. Press → to step. A and B can be workers or ranks in one server.1 · The harness says this is a one-off turn: nothing follows soon.2 · A’s load is only a spike and B’s KV is 92% full, so the router picks no copy, HBM only.3 · B holds S1 in HBM for one request, then drops it. No demotion, no pressure on B’s DRAM.
                  S1 in HBMS1 in DRAMtemporaryfreedother sessions
                  
  
                  
  
                  • No retain: use it once, leave nothing behind.
                  • Harness metadata: session S1, one-off turn, ISL 30k, OSL 500, starts now, no next turn soon.
                  • The router sees A’s load is transient and B’s KV is contended (92% full), so it picks no copy, HBM only.
                  • B’s KVCR pulls S1 into HBM for this request only; it is dropped afterwards and never demoted into B’s DRAM. A and B can be separate workers or ranks in one server.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Primitives · Move
                  Move: copy and invalidate
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  S1 wakes up after ~40 minutes idle. Press → to step.1 · The harness reports the wake-up: 120k of context, resuming now.2 · A is busy and B is idle, and the session needs one home: the router picks move.3 · KVCR copies S1 from A’s G2 to B’s G2, and B loads it into HBM.4 · A invalidates its G1 and G2 copies. The harness gave the event; the router inferred the move.
                  S1 in HBMS1 in DRAMtemporaryfreedother sessions
                  
  
                  
  
                  • Move: copy and invalidate.
                  • Harness metadata: session S1, event wake-up, ISL 120k, OSL 1k, idle ~40 min, resumes now.
                  • The router sees A busy and B idle, and the session needs one home, so it picks move.
                  • KVCR copies S1 to B’s G2 and B loads it into HBM; then A frees its G1 and G2 copies. The harness gives the event; the router infers move.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Primitives · Prefetch
                  Prefetch: copy ahead to a worker with room
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  The harness knows S1’s next turn is about 2 seconds away. Press → to step.1 · The harness signals the next turn: 64k of context, in ~2 s.2 · A is busy and B has room, so the router sends a prefetch hint before the request arrives.3 · KVCR copies S1 into B’s DRAM ahead of time. B loads it into HBM when the request lands.
                  S1 in HBMS1 in DRAMtemporaryfreedother sessions
                  
  
                  
  
                  • Prefetch: copy ahead to a worker with room.
                  • Harness metadata: session S1, next turn expected, ISL 64k, OSL 1k, in ~2 s.
                  • The router sees A busy and low KV pressure on B, so it picks a prefetch copy to B, sent as a hint ahead of the request.
                  • KVCR copies S1 from A’s G2 to B’s G2 before the request; B loads it into HBM at request time.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Primitives · Topology-aware
                  Topology-aware: KVCR inside an RDMA domain
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  A sub-agent forks S1, which lives on busy W1. Press → to step.1 · The harness spawns a sub-agent from S1.2 · W1 is busy. W2 shares its RDMA domain; W3 and W4 are idle but have no fast path. The router picks W2.3 · KVCR copies S1 to W2 inside domain D1.
                  S1 in HBMS1 in DRAMtemporaryfreedother sessions
                  
  
                  
  
                  • Topology-aware: KVCR inside an RDMA domain.
                  • Harness metadata: session S1, sub-agent fork, ISL 48k, OSL 2k, starts now, runs ~30 s.
                  • W1 holds S1 but is busy. W2 is in the same RDMA domain (D1) and free; W3 and W4 on server H2 (domain D2) are idle but have no fast path, so they are not picked.
                  • The router picks W2 and KVCR copies S1 inside D1.
                  

                  



                  

                  

                  



                  


                  
  
                  
    
                  
      Dynamo · Developer intro
      
                  Dynamo
                  
      
                  Open-source, distributed inference serving for the datacenter.
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  • Developer introduction to Dynamo: what it is, why it matters, where it is today, and a tour of its components. Each component slide links to its deep-dive deck on ai-dynamo.org/slides.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  What is Dynamo
                  Engines optimize the GPU. Dynamo optimizes the system around them.
                  
  
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  Open sourceRust + Python · Apache 2.0 · pip, containers, Kubernetes
                  
      
                  Any enginevLLM · SGLang · TensorRT-LLM, and more
                  
      
                  Modularscheduling, memory, data transfer as separate crates and wheels
                  
      
                  Solves: disaggregation · config search · traffic spikes · fault tolerance beyond Kubernetes
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  • Dynamo is an open-source, high-throughput, low-latency inference framework for generative AI in distributed environments (docs, Introduction).
                  • It takes an operating-systems approach: foundations for scheduling, memory management and data transfer, shipped as Rust crates and pip wheels that work together but can be adopted separately. No vendor lock-in.
                  • Problems it addresses: engines only optimize a single forward pass; disaggregated prefill/decode needs scheduling, KV memory management and fast transfer; parallelism configs take days of sweeps; static configs fail on traffic spikes; LLM serving needs fault tolerance beyond standard Kubernetes.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  What Dynamo focuses on
                  How Dynamo approaches performance, scale and resiliency
                  
  
                  Performance
                  

                  2×tokens/s · disagg vs agg
                  agg
                  disagg
                  Baseten · GLM-5.2
                  ⇢
                  Route to the cacheKV events → the worker holding the prefix
                  ⇄
                  Split prefill and decodeeach phase on its own GPUs
                  ▤
                  Keep KV, don't recomputeoffload to host, disk, remote
                  Scalability
                  

                  5×faster cold start
                  before
                  Dynamo
                  Photoroom · Snapshot · 220 s → 40 s
                  ⚡
                  Start in secondsSnapshot + ModelExpress
                  ◎
                  Scale to the SLAPlanner sizes prefill and decode separately
                  ▦

                  Resiliency
                  

                  2.7×faster P95 TTFT in failover
                  before
                  Dynamo
                  KVCR-Guard · internal
                  ⛨
                  Keep state aliveKV and weights outlive the engine
                  ◉
                  Detect fastinhibition, discovery, canaries
                  ↻
                  Keep streams alivemigrate requests with their tokens
                  
  
                  • Performance: Dynamo makes the engine do less work per token. The router sees exactly which KV blocks each worker holds (KV events) and weighs that against load; prefill and decode can run on separate pools; KV is offloaded to cheaper tiers instead of evicted. Proof (published): Baseten, GLM-5.2: "we observed 2x higher tokens per second on disaggregated inference" vs aggregated (head-to-head; hardware not stated).
                  • Scalability: Planner autoscales prefill and decode separately against TTFT/ITL targets; Grove gang-schedules whole multi-node instances with topology awareness; Snapshot and ModelExpress make new workers serve in seconds. Proof (published): Photoroom cut GPU cold starts from ~220 s to 35–45 s with Dynamo Snapshot.
                  • Resiliency: failures are routine at scale. Bad workers are detected in seconds (inhibition, discovery, canaries); in-flight streams migrate with their tokens; every router replica is active and rebuilds from worker events; KVCR-Guard and GMS keep KV and weights through engine crashes. Proof (internal benchmark): KVCR-Guard P95 TTFT during failover 26.5 s → 9.65 s.

                  Scheduling & scaling
                  Snapshot: warm workers in seconds
                  
  
                  
    
                  Checkpoint a warmed-up worker once, including GPU state, and restore it anywhere in seconds.
                  
    
                  • 1
                    Capture a warm workerafter engine init, CRIU + cuda-checkpoint save CPU and GPU state
                  • 2
                    Restore from storageany node resumes the snapshot: seconds instead of a full cold start
                  • 3
                    Weights via ModelExpressrestored nodes pull weights GPU → GPU from a peer
                  
    
                  PhotoroomGPU cold start
                  5× faster
                  Qwen3-Next-80Bto serving, + ModelExpress
                  13× faster
                  Published results gray = before · green = with DynamoDeep dive: mx-snapshot.html →
                  
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  KVCR
                  KVCR: move KV to where it is needed
                  
  
                  
    
                  The router plans where KV should be; KVCR moves it across workers, host memory and storage, and keeps it through engine crashes.
                  
    
                  • 1
                    Router plans the movehints say what to copy, move, prefetch or drop (experimental)
                  • 2
                    KV across nodes and tiersallocate KV across DRAM and storage, peer to peer over NIXL
                  • 3
                    KVCR-Guarda sidecar process holds the KV pool and serves it if the engine fails
                  
    
                  KVCR 0.1.1 early releaseRouter-to-KVCR hints experimental, Dynamo 1.5KVCR-Guard in development
                  
  
                  The whole picture in one slide: the router decides where KV should be, KVCR on each worker moves it peer to peer over NIXL across hosts and tiers, and a KVCR-Guard sidecar keeps the host pool alive when the engine dies. In the demo, B pulls pages from A’s host pool: the dashed arrow. Next, the case it is for: a subagent whose context sits on a busy worker.
                  Maturity, as on the strip: KVCR is an early release (0.1.1 on PyPI), router hints are experimental, Guard is in development and comes back in resiliency.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Memory management
                  GMS: weights that outlive the engine
                  
  
                  
    
                  Model weights live in GPU memory owned by a service, so they outlive the engine process.
                  
    
                  • 1
                    One copy of weightsowned by GMS, mapped read-only into engines
                  • 2
                    Shadow engineparked; takes over in seconds if the active engine crashes
                  • 3
                    Engines plug incustom PyTorch allocator on CUDA VMM
                  
    
                  After an engine crashweights reloaded
                  0 GB
                  gpt-oss-120brestore with GMS + NVMe (PoC)
                  < 5 s
                  Key factsDeep dive: ft.html →
                  
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Memory management
                  FlexTensor: stream weights into HBM on demand
                  
  
                  
    
                  Streams model weights (tensors) from host DRAM into GPU HBM just before each layer runs, so models larger than HBM fit and run at full speed.
                  
    
                  • 1
                    Wrap, don't rewriteplain PyTorch: wrap the nn.Module, no model or engine changes
                  • 2
                    Weights (tensors) in host DRAMpacked into pinned blocks, freeing HBM for KV and activations
                  • 3
                    Streamed just in timeprofiled prefetch hides the copy behind compute
                  
    
                  LTX-2.3 outpaint · A100 80GBmax video length
                  +48.5% longer
                  LTX-2.3 outpaint · 8×A100 80GBmedian generation time
                  2.24× faster
                  Results gray = before · green = with DynamoDeep dive: flextensor.html →
                  
  
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Data transfer
                  NIXL: one API for every transfer
                  
  
                  
    
                  The inference transfer library: one API every engine (vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM) uses to move KV and weights over networks and to storage.
                  
    
                  • 1
                    One async agentpoint to point, non-blocking; used by vLLM, SGLang and TRT-LLM
                  • 2
                    Pluggable backendsnetwork: UCX, libfabric, UCCL, GPUNetIO · storage: GDS, POSIX, 3FS, S3…
                  • 3
                    Every memory tierGPU, CPU, SSD and remote storage behind one API
                  
    
                  VAST DataTTFT · KV from storage vs recompute
                  20× faster
                  CloudianP95 TTFT at 120K tokens · S3 over RDMA vs recompute
                  20× faster
                  Published results gray = before · green = with Dynamo
                  
  
                  ModelExpress decides which GPU holds the weights; NIXL moves the bytes. The same library carries the KV cache from prefill to decode in disaggregation and between KVCR host pools, so this is the one place we introduce it.
                  In our demo NIXL runs its libfabric backend over EFA, eight rails per TP rank: 39.22 GB per GPU in 1.6 to 6.2 s across the three live runs. The storage side of the slide is outside the demo, and the two 20× cards are the partners’ published KV-from-storage results, not workshop measurements.
                  

                  



                  
  
                  Data transfer
                  ModelExpress: weights from peers, not storage
                  
  
                  
    
                  New workers get weights from GPUs that already have them, over NIXL. Storage is read once per cluster.
                  
    
                  • 1
                    Read storage onceone seed per cluster, storage as fallback
                  • 2
                    Peer to peerGPU → GPU over NIXL / RDMA
                  • 3
                    Fan outevery new worker becomes a source

    # pass context → child is linked
    await self.client.generate(

                  Inhibition · discovery · canaries inhibition + discovery oncanaries opt-in
                  Stop sending traffic to a dead or hung worker
                  
  
                  
    
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  1Local inhibition
                  First failed request → the Frontend skips that worker for 5 s. Instant, no coordination.
                  DYN_RUNTIME_INHIBITED_DURATION_SECS=5
                  
      
                  2Discovery
                  Authoritative removal: Kubernetes EndpointSlice update, or the etcd lease expires when keep-alives stop.
                  DYN_DISCOVERY_BACKEND=kubernetes | etcd
                  
      
                  3Canary health check
                  Idle 10 s → send a tiny real inference request, 3 s timeout. Catches an engine that hangs while its process looks alive.
                  DYN_HEALTH_CHECK_ENABLED=true

                  GPU Memory Service preview
                  Weights outlive the engine process
                  
  
                  
    
    
                  
      
                  
        
                  SharedWeights: one copy in HBM, owned by GMS, mapped read-only by every engine. Survives crashes.
                  
        
                  PrivateKV cache, scratch, request state: belong to the active engine. Rebuilt on failover.
                  
        
                  ParkedShadow engine: graphs captured, NCCL ready, weights mapped. Waits on a lock. Costs 4–8 GiB more per GPU.
                  
      
                  
      
                  Built on the CUDA VMM API. vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM plug in through a custom PyTorch allocator.
                  
    
                  
  
                  

                  


                  
  
                  Shadow Engine failover preview
                  Kill the active engine. The shadow takes the lock.

                  Takeaways
                  
  
                  Two problems. Solve both, in parallel.
                  
  
                  
    
                  ModelExpress
                  1×
                  storage read per cluster
                  Moves bytes. Weights flow GPU → GPU from whoever already has them.

                  0 s
                  engine warmup on restore
                  Skips work. Init runs once; every later replica resumes warm.

                  One fast path for cold start, scale-out and recovery.

                  NVIDIA Dynamo · KubernetesDocs baseline: Dynamo v1.5.1
                  
    
                  Planner
                  ×
                  Grove
                  
    
                  Planner decides how many engines to run. Grove decides what one engine instance is and where it lands.
                  
    
                  Interactive: slides 7, 8, 9, 13, 15F full screen← → navigateN notes
                  
  
                  
  
                  What this deck covers. Two pieces of NVIDIA Dynamo's Kubernetes stack and how they work together:
                  

                    

                  • Planner (dynamo.planner): the autoscaler. It decides how many prefill and decode engines a deployment should run.
                    • 

                  • Grove (ai-dynamo/grove): a Kubernetes API (PodCliqueSet, PodCliqueScalingGroup, PodClique, PodGang) that turns those counts into complete, gang‑scheduled model instances.
                    • 

                  

                  Sources. Behaviour is taken from the Dynamo v1.5.1 docs and checked against the Planner source on main (commit 7b0e63e) and the Grove API reference.
                  

                  Flow. Slides 2–3 set up the problem, 4–9 explain Planner, 10–11 show the hand‑off to Kubernetes, 12–14 explain Grove, 15 ties it together in a simulator, 16–17 cover scale‑out and operations.
                  

                  Keys. ← → navigate · F full screen · N toggles these notes.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  The problem
                  
    
                  Three problems a generic autoscaler can’t solve for LLM serving
                  
    
  
                  
  
                  Point of the slide: frame the three problems Dynamo has to solve. A CPU‑ or pod‑count autoscaler (e.g. a plain HPA) solves none of them. Each panel ends with what a solution needs; slide 3 shows which component provides it.
                  

                    

                  • Two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is compute‑bound; it determines time to first token (TTFT). Decode generates one token per step and is memory‑bandwidth‑bound; it determines inter‑token latency (ITL). In disaggregated serving they run on separate workers, so each needs its own replica count.
                    • 

                  • Demand is tokens. 10 req/s at ISL 8,000 is 16× the prefill work of ISL 500. Planner therefore forecasts ISL/OSL alongside request count, discounts ISL by the KV‑cache hit rate, and evaluates decode at context length ISL + OSL/2.
                    • 

                  • The unit of capacity can span nodes. A TP16 decode instance is two 8‑GPU pods. In a DGD this is multinode.nodeCount: 2 with gpu: 8 per node (total GPUs = nodeCount × gpu). Half an instance serves nothing, so capacity must be added in whole units.
                    • 

                  

                  Problems ① and ② are solved by Planner; problem ③ by Grove (next slide).
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  PlannerGrove
                  
    
                  How Dynamo solves them: Planner + Grove
                  
    
  
                  
  
                  Maps the problems to components. Planner solves ① (separate prefill/decode counts sized on TTFT/ITL) and ② (forecasts request count, ISL and OSL, not just request rate). Grove solves ③ (adds and removes whole multi‑node instances, placed all‑or‑nothing).
                  

                  Planner runs as a service inside the DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD), componentType: planner.
                  

                    

                  • Inputs: Prometheus traffic metrics from the Frontend (dynamo_frontend_*) or a router, plus per‑iteration Forward Pass Metrics (FPM) that engines publish on the event plane.
                    • 

                  • Output: a replica count per role. The KubernetesConnector finds its parent DGD via DYN_PARENT_DGD_K8S_NAME, resolves services by subComponentType (prefill/decode) and patches spec.services[x].replicas.
                    • 

                  

                  Grove never receives a call from Planner. The Dynamo operator reconciles the DGD into Grove resources, and Grove plus KAI Scheduler place the pods.
                  

                  So the DGD replica count is the contract. Anything that writes it (Planner, HPA/KEDA through a scaling adapter, a human) is handled the same way downstream.
                  

                  Other connectors: virtual (non‑Kubernetes orchestrators poll decisions) and global-planner (slide 16).
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  PlannerHow it works today
                  
    
                  Planner runs one pipeline every tick
                  
    
    
                  Perf model from the first available:self‑benchmark→AI Configurator→profiling data→live FPM regression
                  
    
                  Which proposers run depends onoptimization_target(next slide) ·advisory: truerecommends without scaling
                  
  
                  
  
                  The runtime is driven by OrchestratorEngineAdapter. Each tick runs a fixed pipeline:
                  

                    

                  1. Observe: worker counts, traffic metrics, FPM.
                    2. 

                  2. Predict: builtin_load_predict forecasts next‑interval request count, ISL and OSL.
                    3. 

                  3. Propose: builtin_throughput_propose (forecast → floor) and builtin_load_propose (live ±1). External gRPC plugins can propose too.
                    4. 

                  4. Reconcile / constrain: merge proposals, apply minimums and the GPU budget.
                    5. 

                  5. Execute: PlannerEffects.scale_to goes to the connector.
                    6. 

                  

                  Cadence. The base tick (scheduling.scale_interval_seconds) defaults to the GCD of the enabled loop intervals, normally 5 s. Each plugin fires only when its own interval has elapsed.
                  

                  Perf model. Capacity estimates come from a forward‑pass performance model (AISimulate). It is bootstrapped from the first available of: worker self‑benchmark, AI Configurator simulation (pre_deployment_sweeping_mode: rapid, default), real‑GPU profiling (thorough, 2–4 h), or live FPM regression. It keeps tuning itself from live FPM.
                  

                  Advisory mode (advisory: true) runs everything but skips Execute; recommendations appear as dynamo_planner_* metrics, HTML reports and a live dashboard (port 8080).
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
    
                  Planner scaling policies
                  
    
  
                  
  
                  Planner scaling policies (1.5 min)
                  

                  We choose between these two approaches with the Planner's optimization target setting.
                  

                  On the left, we scale from engine load. The Planner checks queued prefill tokens and decode KV demand. That demand can include queued work, which is why the scale can go above a hundred percent. It isn't simply the fraction of physical cache blocks occupied.
                  

                  The throughput preset tolerates more queueing before adding capacity. The latency preset scales earlier. With the load policy, we choose the scale-up and scale-down thresholds ourselves. By default, these checks run every five seconds.
                  

                  On the right, SLA mode starts from latency targets. In this example, we want time to first token within five hundred milliseconds and inter-token latency within fifty milliseconds.
                  

                  The forecast loop runs every three minutes by default and sets a minimum replica count for predicted demand. We can also enable a reactive loop that checks every five seconds and can adjust the count by one replica. It uses latency estimates from engine metrics and the performance model, so we still need to check the actual latency our clients experience.
                  

                  These targets guide scaling decisions. Whether we meet them depends on the workload, available capacity and how quickly new workers become ready.
                  

                  Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):
                  

                  • This slide has no manual animation steps; do not add CLICK cues.
                  

                  • The spoken name 'optimization target' refers to the optimization_target field. SLA mode is optimization_target: sla; the optional reactive loop is enable_load_scaling.
                  

                  • Default loop intervals are 5 seconds for load checks and 180 seconds for the SLA predictive loop. Preset thresholds are version-specific.

                  Plannersla target with load scaling on · both loops
                  
    
                  How Planner makes the autoscaling decision
                  
    
                  
      
                  1 · every 180 s
                  Forecast a floor
                  
        
                  floor = ⌈ forecast req/s
                  ÷ req/s one engine
                    serves at the SLA ⌉
                  
        
                  Capacity is ready before the demand arrives.

                  ▲ +1 every engine over SLA
                  ▼ −1 load fits on N−1 engines
                  ● hold otherwise
                  
        
                  Estimated per engine from forward‑pass metrics.
                  
      
                  3 · combine
                  Never below the floor

                  The four steps Planner applies in sla mode with load scaling enabled.
                  

                    

                  1. Forecast floor (every 180 s, throughput_adjustment_interval_seconds). floor = ⌈forecast req/s ÷ req/s one engine serves within the SLA⌉. Each step moves at most ±8 replicas (max_throughput_scaling_replicas).
                    2. 

                  2. Live check (every 5 s, load_adjustment_interval_seconds). Per engine, estimate TTFT/ITL from FPM. +1 if every engine is over the SLA. −1 only if, after removing one engine (load × N/(N−1)), every engine still fits (slide 8). Otherwise hold.
                    3. 

                  3. Combine. desired = max(live decision, floor). The live loop can add above the floor but never cut below it, so a short lull doesn't remove capacity the forecast says is coming.
                    4. 

                  4. Guardrails. No scale‑up while replicas are still starting (scale‑down may cancel starting ones). Never below min_endpoint. At max_gpu_budget a scale‑up is held; forecast targets over budget are clamped proportionally (prefill floored first, decode gets the remainder).
                    5. 

                  

                  The chart is a stylised illustration of steps 1–3 during a burst, not real data.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  PlannerPredictive loop · optimization_target: sla
                  
    
                  How the throughput loop picks a replica count
                  
    
                  
      
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  Engines: prefill TP2 (2 GPUs), decode TP4 (4 GPUs). Curves are illustrative; real ones come from self‑benchmark, AI Configurator or profiling.
                  
      
                  
      
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  Worked example of step 1 (core/state_machine.py, core/throughput_scaling.py, core/perf_model/engine_query.py).
                  

                    

                  1. Forecast. Prometheus gives the last 180 s: request count, avg ISL, avg OSL (Frontend metrics), KV hit rate (router), spec‑decode accept length (engine). ARIMA (default; also constant, kalman, prophet) forecasts request count, ISL and OSL. KV hit and accept length reuse the last value. demand_rps = predicted num_req ÷ interval.
                    2. 

                  2. Capacity per engine. find_engine_capacity_rps queries the perf model. Prefill: ISL × (1 − KV hit, capped at 0.95); scans batch sizes, rps = batch ÷ TTFT, eligible if TTFT ≤ SLA. Decode: context = ISL + OSL/2; ITL = forward time ÷ accept length; rps = batch ÷ (OSL × ITL), eligible if ITL ≤ SLA. Highest eligible rps wins. If none meets the SLA it returns the best effort and logs a warning.
                    3. 

                  3. Divide. replicas = ⌈demand_rps ÷ engine_rps⌉, at least min_endpoint.
                    4. 

                  4. Constrain. Compare total GPUs with max_gpu_budget; clamp proportionally if over.
                    5. 

                  

                  The sliders drive an illustrative curve (latency = base ÷ (1 − load)); real curves come from the perf model. If the model isn't ready, Planner holds the current count (model_not_ready).
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  PlannerReactive loop · sla mode
                  
    
                  How the load loop decides +1, −1 or hold
                  
    
                  
      
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  Shown for prefill/TTFT. Decode uses scheduled + queued KV tokens → ITL (÷ accept length). ±1 per tick; no scale‑up while replicas are starting; never below the throughput floor.
                  
      
                  
      
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  Worked example of step 2 (core/load_scaling.py, _scale_decision).
                  

                    

                  1. Learn from forward passes. Engines emit FPM per iteration: wall_time, scheduled and queued prefill tokens, decode KV tokens, request counts. These tune the AISimulate perf model (up to max_num_fpm_samples = 64; ready after load_min_observations = 5). The scatter and straight‑line fit on the slide are a simplification.
                    2. 

                  2. Simulate the queue. TTFT for a new request = queued prefill tokens × (1 − KV hit) + its own ISL, split into chunks of max_num_batched_tokens, each chunk's forward time summed. ITL uses scheduled + queued decode KV, divided by accept length.
                    3. 

                  3. Decide. +1 if every engine's estimate > SLA. −1 only if, with load × N/(N−1), each engine's queue delay stays under (ttft_ms − own time) × load_scaling_down_sensitivity/100 (default 80). For decode: post‑consolidation KV must fit and ITL < itl_ms × sensitivity.
                    4. 

                  

                  Hollow dots show each engine's estimate if one engine were removed. Try the imbalance slider: one hot engine is enough to block both scale‑up (not all over) and scale‑down.

                  Interactive timeline. One simulated hour; the same rules from slides 6–8 applied tick by tick.
                  

                    

                  • Top: observed req/s (green) and the 180 s forecasts (amber dashes).
                    •

                  Simplifications: prefill engine = 2 GPUs serving 9.1 req/s at SLA; decode engine = 4 GPUs serving 21 req/s; budget 40 GPUs; ARIMA approximated by a trend fit; threshold signals modelled from utilisation. Flapping in default mode under steady traffic is an artifact of that model.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  PlannerGroveActuation path
                  
    
                  One scale decision, end to end
                  
    
  
                  
  
                  The full actuation path for one decision (decode 2 → 3):
                  

                    

                  1. Planner calls set_component_replicas().
                    2. 

                  2. DGD spec.services.decode.replicas becomes 3. If the service has scalingAdapter enabled, a DynamoGraphDeploymentScalingAdapter (DGDSA) owns replicas via the Scale subresource, and a webhook blocks direct edits. Use one autoscaler per service (Planner or HPA/KEDA).
                    3. 

                  3. Dynamo operator reconciles the DGD into Grove resources.
                    4. 

                  4. Grove raises the PodCliqueScalingGroup to 3 and creates a new scaled PodGang.
                    5. 

                  5. KAI Scheduler binds the PodGang all‑or‑nothing, honouring topology constraints; if it can't fit, it stays Pending.
                    6. 

                  6. Pods start in the declared order (startsAfter), register with Dynamo discovery, and Planner sees them as ready capacity.
                    7. 

                  

                  Inspect it: kubectl get dgd,dgdsa then kubectl get pcs,pcsg,pclq,pg,pod.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  GroveResource mapping
                  
    
                  What Planner’s number actually scales
                  
    
    
                  replicas = complete instances · nodeCount = pods per instance · each instance = one PodGang
                  
  
                  
  
                  How the DGD you write becomes Grove objects (Grove is the default multinode orchestrator; set nvidia.com/enable-grove: "false" to use LWS + Volcano).
                  

                    

                  • One DGD → one PodCliqueSet.
                    • 

                  • Single‑node service (e.g. prefill, 1 pod per engine) → one PodClique; replicas = number of pods.
                    • 

                  • Multinode service → one PodCliqueScalingGroup with a leader PodClique and a worker PodClique. replicas = complete instances; multinode.nodeCount = pods per instance (1 leader + nodeCount − 1 workers).
                    • 

                  • GPUs per instance = nodeCount × gpu; the engine's TP size must match (16 here).
                    • 

                  

                  Planner's replica number therefore lands on a PodClique for single‑node roles and on a PodCliqueScalingGroup for multinode roles. Grove also supports scaling the whole PodCliqueSet (service copies) and individual PodCliques.
                  

                  Resource names on the slide are illustrative; the operator derives them from DGD and service names.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  LeaderWorkerSetGroveSame service, two views
                  
    
                  What does the scheduler treat as “one unit”?
                  
    
                  Example service: 2 prefill + 1 decode instances, each instance = a leader pod + a worker pod.
                  
    
    
                  
      
                  LWSGrove
                  
      
                  Leader + workers of one instance placed together✓✓
                  
      
                  Prefill + decode placed together (a service that can actually answer)✗✓
                  
      
                  Startup order across roleswithin a group✓
                  
      
                  Scale one role without touching the other✓✓
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  Same service drawn twice: 2 prefill instances and 1 decode instance, each a leader + worker pod.
                  

                  LeaderWorkerSet (kubernetes‑sigs/lws) models one multi‑pod role well: each group (leader + workers) can be gang‑scheduled by Volcano or KAI. A disaggregated service needs one LWS per role, and nothing links them, so the scheduler sees three independent units. Startup ordering (LeaderCreated / LeaderReady) applies only inside a group.
                  

                  Grove describes the whole service as one PodCliqueSet and builds PodGangs from it:
                  

                    

                  • Base PodGang (API role Anchor): all standalone PodCliques plus the first minAvailable replicas of each PodCliqueScalingGroup. Placed all‑or‑nothing: the smallest service that can answer a request.
                    • 

                  • Scaled PodGangs (role Tail): one per replica above minAvailable, each gang‑scheduled on its own.
                    • 

                  • minAvailable also drives gang termination: if a group falls below it for longer than TerminationDelay, the gang is torn down and rescheduled.
                    • 

                  • Cross‑role startup order: cliqueStartupType AnyOrder (default), InOrder, or Explicit with startsAfter.
                    • 

                  

                  LWS remains a good fit for single‑role multi‑node serving; the gap is cross‑role viability.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  LeaderWorkerSetGroveInteractive · step through
                  
    
                  Why it matters when GPUs are scarce
                  
    
                  
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
                  
    
                  
    
                  
      
                  LeaderWorkerSet
                  
      
                  Grove
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  Step through two scenarios with ◀ / ▶. Assumptions: 6 nodes; each prefill or decode instance needs 2 nodes (leader + worker); LWS groups are gang‑scheduled one at a time in arrival order; Grove schedules each base PodGang as one unit.
                  

                  ① Tight capacity (3 free nodes, service needs 4). LWS places prefill because that group fits, then decode waits: 16 GPUs are held and no request can be served (prefill has nowhere to send KV). Grove places nothing, so the 3 nodes stay available to other work, then places all 4 pods together when a node frees.
                  

                  ② Two services race (4 free nodes, A and B each need 4). LWS places A·prefill, then B·prefill, and both decodes wait forever: a resource deadlock with 32 GPUs held and both services down. Grove places A whole; B waits cleanly.
                  

                  Scale‑out of an already running service behaves the same in both systems (one new gang per instance). The difference is only the cross‑role base gang.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  GroveOn every scale event
                  
    
                  Scale‑out adds a complete instance
                  
    
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  Gang scheduling
                  Whole instance or nothing
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  Hierarchical gangs
                  Never prefill without decode
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  Startup ordering
                  Roles start in declared order
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  Topology‑aware
                  Set via topologyConstraint

                  Capacity count stays honest
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
        
                  Coherent updates
                  Prefill + decode roll together
                  
      
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                  Summary of what Grove adds to every scale event Planner triggers:
                  

                    

                  • Gang scheduling: each instance is a PodGang; all pods bind or none do.
                    • 

                  • Hierarchical gangs: the base PodGang guarantees a viable service (≥ 1 prefill + ≥ 1 decode) before extras.
                    • 

                  • Startup ordering: cliqueStartupType / startsAfter, e.g. workers before leader (MPI) or router before workers.
                    • 

                  • Topology‑aware placement: pack an instance within a rack, block or NVLink domain; spread replicas for availability. Exposed on the DGD as topologyConstraint; a PCSG constraint must be equal to or stricter than the PodCliqueSet's.
                    • 

                  • Gang termination: below minAvailable (after TerminationDelay), the gang is removed as a unit, so Planner's ready count reflects real serving capacity.
                    • 

                  • Coherent updates: select the PodCliqueSet update strategy from the DGD with nvidia.com/grove-update-strategy (RollingRecreate or OnDelete).
                    • 

                  

                  Version pairing for Dynamo 1.5.x: KAI Scheduler ≥ v0.17.0, Grove ≥ v0.1.0‑alpha.13 when installed separately.

                  • Controls: traffic pattern, peak req/s, ISL/OSL, TTFT/ITL SLA, GPU budget, decode shape (TP16 two‑node PCSG vs TP4 single‑pod PodClique), loop toggles, speed.

                  PlannerBeyond one DGD
                  
    
                  One Planner per DGD; GlobalPlanner coordinates many
                  
    
  
                  
  
                  A local Planner manages exactly one DGD. GlobalPlanner centralises scaling across several.
                  

                    

                  • Pattern 1 · shared policy: independent DGDs (often different models) keep their own endpoints. Each local Planner sets environment: global-planner and global_planner_namespace; GlobalPlanner authorises callers (--managed-namespaces) and enforces a total budget (--max-total-gpus). No GlobalRouter needed.
                    • 

                  • Pattern 2 · one endpoint, many pools (shown): a control DGD (Frontend + GlobalRouter + GlobalPlanner) fronts private pool DGDs. GlobalRouter picks a prefill pool by ISL and TTFT target, and a decode pool by context length and ITL target. Pool Planners must use throughput_metrics_source: router so they forecast from their own LocalRouter.
                    • 

                  

                  Grove is unchanged: each pool DGD is its own PodCliqueSet with its own gangs.
                  

                  Limitation today: one DGDR does not generate the multi‑pool topology; profile each pool separately and compose the DGDs by hand.
                  

                  




                  
  
                  
    
                  Operating notes
                  
    
                  Things that bite in practice
                  
    
                  
      
                  Δt
                  Interval ≥ time‑to‑ready
                  Otherwise ticks just hold. Multinode gangs are slowest.
                  
      
                  μ
                  Averages hide tails
                  Bimodal ISL? Split into pools under GlobalPlanner.
                  
      
                  1
                  One autoscaler per service
                  HPA on Frontend + Planner on workers. Never both on decode.
                  
      
                  ≥1
                  No scale‑to‑zero
                  Zero workers = model leaves /v1/models, no signal to return.
                  
      
                  ≠
                  Budget ≠ cluster
                  Planner caps the ask; KAI decides what fits. Misfits stay Pending.
                  
      
                  1.5
                  Version pairing
                  KAI ≥ v0.17.0 · Grove ≥ v0.1.0‑alpha.13 when installed externally.
                  
    
                  
  
                  
  
                    

                  • Interval ≥ time‑to‑ready. If an interval is shorter than scheduling + model load + registration, ticks see a transition in progress and hold. Multinode gangs are slowest; size throughput_adjustment_interval_seconds accordingly.
                    • 

                  • Averages hide tails. The forecast uses mean ISL/OSL. For bimodal traffic, split into pools behind GlobalPlanner.
                    • 

                  • One autoscaler per service. HPA/KEDA on the Frontend plus Planner on workers is fine; two autoscalers on decode will fight.
                    • 

                  • No scale‑to‑zero for workers. With zero workers the model disappears from /v1/models, so there is no demand signal to scale back up. Keep min 1.
                    • 

                  • Budget ≠ cluster capacity. max_gpu_budget (default 8) caps what Planner asks for; KAI decides what fits. A gang that doesn't fit stays Pending and Planner holds that role.
                    • 

                  • Version pairing. Dynamo 1.5.x with external installs: KAI ≥ v0.17.0, Grove ≥ v0.1.0‑alpha.13.
                    • 

                  

                  Useful signals: dynamo_planner_estimated_ttft_ms, dynamo_planner_estimated_itl_ms, dynamo_planner_predicted_num_prefill_replicas/_decode_replicas, and the load‑scaling decision enum.
